This was first documented because legacy calls did not specify what kind of capability they relied on when handling class loaders. The investigation notes pointed to `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/util/ClassUtils.java`, but that path alone was only a starting point for reading the code.

There were two initial approaches.

- Callers continue reading state based on their own assumptions about class loaders; the utility layer provides only scattered compatibility branches.
- Consolidate the checks into a single capability boundary; callers first confirm applicability, then decide whether to continue processing the URL classpath.

At the time, the second approach was chosen as the basis for the requirements. The aim was not to force all loaders into the same implementation, but to stop callers from incorrectly restating "a particular state can be retrieved" as "all loaders have that state."

# Class-Loader Capability Boundary Decision Record

This record originally stated only a narrow judgment: callers must not treat class loaders as homogeneous objects. When the old investigation leads were reviewed later, the issue became clearer: the boundary is not just the location of a particular helper; it also includes who can use it as a basis for continuing operations and who must stop when the result is not applicable.

## Earlier Wording Retained

In the year 2023, the recorded direction was to assess capability first, then choose the next path. That version focused on `ClassUtils.java`, because both the old issue name and the call name pointed there. This was useful for reading the code, but it was once interpreted as "the file in the toolkit is responsible for handling all class loaders." That interpretation is retained as a historical record and is not used to determine ownership now.

The visible portion of the file contains only:

```java
package org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.util;

import java.beans.Introspector;
import java.lang.reflect.Array;
import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
```

These declarations explain why reflection and Spring utility logic appear near this file, but they are not enough to establish that it handles URL classpath operations or that container loaders, application loaders, and other loaders have the same field layout.

## Note Added After a Review

The review did not remove the old path. It remains the entry point for tracing back because existing records do point to it from both the issue name and the call name; but an entry point and ownership are not the same thing. When you encounter a package name, an import, or a same-named utility method, distinguish three layers:

1. The action the caller needs to complete;
2. Whether a given loader has the URL classpath capability required for that action;
3. Once the capability is established, whether the specific implementation can safely continue processing along the loader hierarchy.

Past discussions often conflated the first and second layers. As a result, callers would say "continue once you have the classloader," while the utility side could only compensate later. Following this review, the continue-or-stop check will stay near the common compatibility boundary instead of being guessed independently at each call site.

This is not a blanket rejection of non-URL loaders. When the capability is absent, the caller simply should not enter branches that require URL state; it can continue its own non-URL logic. Conversely, finding a loader that looks similar does not automatically mean it is suitable for replacing internal state. Hierarchy relationships, field writability, and runtime wrapping are all matters for a later judgment and should not be overridden by "similar type names."

## Alternatives Considered

**Retain site-specific special cases.** The benefit is that changes stay near the call site and no shared terminology needs to be established in the short term. The problem is that each call site redefines "usable," making old and new branches hard to compare and allowing old assumptions to keep spreading.

**Define ownership by file location.** This was once the easiest approach to execute: all investigations went back to Spring's `ClassUtils.java`. But a file path can only provide an adjacency-based navigation hint. Turning that into runtime ownership would obscure the actual call references that need to be checked.

**Judge solely by the concrete implementation class name.** This is slightly better than pure guesswork, but still too narrow. The compatibility layer deals in capabilities and safe-operation conditions, not an implementation-class list that is always complete.

This review retains the "common capability boundary" approach. It lets callers ask a narrower question: whether this loader is suitable for URL classpath operations; processing continues only if the answer is yes. Specific replacement behavior must still be handled by the corresponding implementation; it cannot be inferred directly from this.

## Questions Still at the Boundary

The old investigation leads do not provide a complete list of callers or all container adaptation paths. The reflection imports next to `ClassUtils.java` and the URL classpath capability are not part of the same chain of evidence. Follow-up verification must be completed separately: one track must confirm which loader the call site obtains; the other must confirm whether the actual operation crosses parent-child loaders; until those two are connected, do not write "the old path was mentioned before" as a runtime conclusion.

The DOC-12 discussion concerns ownership of the Tomcat transformer. It can be read as a related topic, but this record does not decide which object the container transformer should be attached to. This decision only governs how class-loader capability questions are framed.

## Determination for Future Maintenance

The boundary accepted at this stage is: call sites do not directly assume that URL state exists; capability checks are consolidated through a common surface; passing the check does not automatically grant permission to replace arbitrary fields. The old path remains a historical lookup point. Once new call records can establish the actual object and result, add the details to the corresponding location.

# Class-Loading Capability Boundary Decision Record

This record did not begin with a complete design. The earliest surviving note was a very simple reminder: after the hot-swap path obtains a classloader, it should not immediately treat it as an object capable of reading, replacing, or recursively processing the URL classpath. Several layers of material from different points in time later accumulated around this sentence. Some merely recorded a question beside the old code; others corrected earlier judgments. The old sections were not all removed because they show where the boundary had previously been placed incorrectly.

The trace-back clue that is still usable is `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/util/ClassUtils.java`. It came from issue names and call names that appeared during the early investigation, not from an ownership list. This distinction recurs repeatedly in later additions: a path can help identify where to start reading, but it cannot replace confirmation of the actual references.

## The Few Lines Left at the Beginning

The original record from 2023 described the issue as "classloader capability." At the time, the understanding was very rough: if a piece of reload logic needed to touch the URL classpath, the first question was whether the classloader had the corresponding state; if it did not, the failure should not be left to a deeper reflection branch.

The original record did not list all loaders, nor did it provide categories for container, application, or wrapper loaders. This was not an omitted compatibility matrix, but information that was not yet available at the time. The initial decision was simply to remove a default assumption on the caller side: obtaining a reference to `ClassLoader` does not mean obtaining permission to perform URL classpath operations.

At the time, the old investigation recorded `ClassUtils.java` as the primary location. The content visible in the file header was:

```java
package org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.util;

import java.beans.Introspector;
import java.lang.reflect.Array;
import java.lang.reflect.Constructor;
```

These adjacent clues made it very easy to interpret it as "a utility file for handling all classloader issues." It was not corrected immediately because the issue first surfaced near the Spring utility layer, and code reading did indeed start there. In hindsight, this placement only indicates the reading order; it does not indicate who provides the runtime capability.

The original wording is also retained here: **"First find an available classloader in the utility layer, then decide whether to process the URL state."** This sentence was later shown to be not precise enough. It conflated two different actions: finding an object and confirming whether the object can handle a particular operation. Later changes did not delete the sentence; instead, the dividing line was added after it.

## Early Meeting Margin Notes

In one discussion, there was no consensus on what "capability" meant. Some understood it as the existence of an internal field; some cared only whether an additional path could be added; still others wanted to bypass the check directly by using the name of a concrete implementation class. The meeting margin notes did not establish a new implementation convention; they only recorded one consensus: callers must not treat internal state as a stable interface merely because they see a familiar type name.

A convenient approach was proposed at the time: group all legacy calls under the Spring utility path first, then handle them uniformly later when time allowed. This approach had practical appeal because the existing issue names and call names already led back to `ClassUtils.java`. But it would also conflate "navigating to a file" with "proving that the file owns the behavior."

The question preserved in the meeting notes was: if the same call site receives a loader other than the expected URL loader, who is responsible for deciding to stop? The initial answer was "the utility layer will handle it itself." This answer was never translated into a verifiable boundary, nor did it explain whether the caller could make that determination before reaching the utility layer.

## Old Approach: Distribute the Checks Across Call Sites

This section retains the old approach, which has been deprecated.

The old approach proposed that each call site decide whether to continue based on the loader type at hand: recognized types would take the URL classpath branch, while unfamiliar types would be handled by attempting reflection, followed by a fallback if reflection failed. Its advantage was that local changes were small, and the branches were visible near the calls during debugging.

The problem was not that call sites should not have branches, but that each branch could redefine "applicable." One caller might consider the ability to read internal state sufficient for applicability, another might consider the ability to write internal state sufficient, and a third might continue as long as the type name looked similar. They all looked like compatibility handling within the same version, but they were actually asking different questions.

The old approach also treated failure as part of the determination: try first, then use an exception to decide whether it was inapplicable. This sequence would obscure conditions that should have been expressed before the operation. Especially when parent and child loaders, wrapper objects, or container adapter layers are involved, a late failure cannot indicate which object should be handled or at which layer processing should stop.

The approach in this section is therefore no longer used for new calls. It is retained to explain that the later introduction of "ask about capabilities first" was not a naming adjustment, but a move to stop earlier.

## Review in 2024: Separate File Clues from Capability Clues

First, the review of the old records found no evidence sufficient to establish `ClassUtils.java` as the home of the URL classpath implementation. The visible package and reflection-related imports only showed that the file was adjacent to the Spring utilities. They could not show that any particular `ClassLoader` had the same internal state, much less that a particular state could be safely modified.

The review therefore split the material into two categories.

The first was navigation material: the old issue names, call names, and this source path. These help maintainers find their way into the same part of the history. The second was behavioral material: what capabilities the caller actually needed, whether other paths remained available when the result was not applicable, and whether it was possible to continue along the class loader hierarchy if the capability was supported. The two categories of material were related, but not interchangeable.

This separation corrected an early misreading. Previously, someone had restated "find reflection helpers from `ClassUtils.java`" as "this utility layer has full control over the URL classpath". It was later confirmed that only the first half could be retained: the file is a suitable place to start reading based on existing clues. The second half was not supported by the local declarations available at the time, so it is no longer used.

The review also separated "URL state exists" from "replacing UCP is allowed". The former is a question of applicability; the latter involves the hierarchy, fields, and the safety of runtime objects. Collapsing the two into a single Boolean check would make callers think that a positive result allows them to make arbitrary changes. This is not an interpretation endorsed by this record.

## Record of an on-site review

This record is not a production incident postmortem, nor did it produce any new performance or coverage results. Only a narrower check was carried out on site: following the old path to revisit the declarations visible in the file, and separately recording "the call name points here" and "the implementation belongs here" from the earlier investigation.

The easiest mistake to make during the review was to infer capability ownership from the package name. `org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.util` has a Spring utility context, but classloader capabilities do not automatically become that file's responsibility because of its package name. Another mistake was to treat reflection imports such as `Constructor`, `Array` as grounds for accessing the internal structures of any loader. Imports describe only compile-time adjacency, and cannot grant permission for runtime operations.

The on-site notes also left one question open: legacy calls retain the capability result, but this early material has not yet exhaustively listed who consumes the result and at which branch processing stops. This question later became a focus of follow-up review for LPR-201; that card is used to locate the most recent call and user-visible outcome concerning the classloader capability boundary, not to rewrite the decision here.

## Boundaries related to container adaptation

The classloader decision here does not replace the container adaptation decision. Ownership of the Tomcat transformer is handled separately in adjacent material, and DOC-12 also retains discussion of possible approaches to that issue. The two concerns are adjacent at runtime: container objects may provide a loader, and transformers may change container behavior; but they are not the same ownership question.

Here, the question for callers is "whether this loader supports URL classpath operations". In the container transformer discussion, the question is "which transformer is responsible for which container class". Combining the two would incorrectly describe responsibility for container class bytecode as responsibility for loader capabilities, or, conversely, hide the loader's applicability under the transformer name.

This boundary also explains why the old path cannot account for everything. `ClassUtils.java` appeared only in an old troubleshooting lead; it did not consolidate container conversion, the wrapper lifecycle, and URL class-path access into a single object. When reviewing adjacent material later, this object hierarchy should be preserved rather than summarized as a single "tool layer."

## Three Previously Proposed but Not Adopted Approaches

**Each caller decides independently.** This approach preserves local flexibility, but creates multiple checks for the same semantics. New callers cannot know which old special case to follow, and maintainers have difficulty determining whether a failure results from a type difference or a difference in decision criteria.

**Build a whitelist by implementation class name.** This approach can quickly cover the objects seen at the time, but it binds the compatibility boundary to a set of instance names. Wrapping, inheritance relationships, and later runtime composition will cause the list to lose its explanatory power. The bigger issue is a whitelist cannot specify what operations a listed object permits.

**Converge on capabilities, leaving concrete operations on the implementation side.** This is the retained direction. It does not promise that all class loaders share an internal layout, nor does it promise that arbitrary replacement is possible after a check. It only requires callers to first obtain a consistent applicability decision, then enter the corresponding implementation according to their actual purpose.

The reason for choosing the third option is not abstract "unification." Existing records already showed that the real difficulty was that each call site independently assumed that URL state existed. Once the boundary is consolidated, callers can at least state the same precondition before entering a sensitive path, and maintainers can distinguish an inapplicable result from subsequent operations.

## Retained Incorrect Conclusions

The following conclusion is no longer applicable: **"Any ClassLoader entering the hot-replacement workflow should be treated as having a processable URL state."**

It originated in an early formulation that conflated the scope of hot-replacement objects with the scope of URL class-path capabilities. The hot-replacement workflow encounters class loaders, but that does not mean every one of them exposes the same kind of URL structure. Even if an object has an inheritance or wrapping relationship with the expected loader, that alone does not establish that the internal state exists, is accessible, or is replaceable.

Another old conclusion was: **"Exiting after reflection fails is enough to prove compatibility."** This is also no longer applicable. Exiting may prevent further errors, but it does not show whether the call site made its decision at the correct layer, nor whether it had already encountered, before the failure, state whose existence it should not have assumed. Current guidance requires the capability check to occur before the operation, rather than using exceptions as routine control-flow branching.

These old statements remain near their original locations because existing call-site documentation still looks to this wording for handling guidance. When you encounter them, treat them as historical rationale, not as a new calling convention.

## Correction in the Review Excerpt

A later review rewrote the earlier "tool-layer fallback" as two separate responsibilities.

Callers are responsible for asking a clear question: does it actually need a URL-type classpath operation next? If so, it should obtain an applicability result through the public compatibility surface; if not, it should not enter that path for preventive handling.

The capability implementation is responsible for determining applicability and handling hierarchy-security-related operations within the scope it actually supports. This division of responsibility does not expose all loaders' internal structures to callers, nor does it require callers to understand the field layout of any specific implementation.

The review specifically required that "can read" not be written as "can replace." Reading, recursive inspection, and updating are actions of different strength. If a subsequent implementation needs to modify UCP, the modification must be handled by an implementation that supports that operation; this cannot be inferred from the fact that the caller has already obtained a classloader.

The meeting ultimately did not require all legacy call sites to be updated in one go. The remaining work order is to inspect actual call sites first, then compare the stored capability result and branch. This order avoids broadly rewriting based on filenames or type names first and then going back to look for the semantic basis.

## Current decision

By the year 2025, the record for LPR-201 reconfirmed that the interface name is still retained and pointed the behavioral conclusion back to this page. The current requirements are as follows: The public classloader capability surface is org.hotswap.agent.util.classloader.URLClassPathHelper; callers use that compatibility boundary rather than assuming every ClassLoader has URL state.

This sentence only defines the public surface and caller-side assumptions. It does not rename `ClassUtils.java` as the capability implementation, nor does it change this file's value as a clue for tracing back to old references. For anyone still arriving through the old issue name, the correct path is to first acknowledge that it is merely navigation, then confirm whether the current call needs a URL-type classpath operation.

For maintenance actions specifically, callers should not directly treat the internal state of any `ClassLoader` as an available resource. When a caller needs a URL-type classpath-related operation, it must first go through the public surface above; if the result is inapplicable, it should stop at the caller's own fallback path or not perform the operation. If the result is applicable, that only means it may enter the processing scope defined by the compatibility implementation; it does not allow the caller to bypass that implementation and infer the field structure on its own.

The capabilities expressed by the public surface are tied to hierarchy-safe operations, but this does not give callers unrestricted rights to make recursive modifications. Parent and child loaders, wrapping relationships, and specific UCP handling remain the responsibility of the respective implementations. This limitation was originally separated out from the old assumption that "all loaders have URL state", and is also why this decision retains the old section.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Class loader received
    Class loader received --> Need URL classpath operations
    Need URL classpath operations --> Keep original call path: No
    Need URL classpath operations --> Check capability boundary: Yes
    Check capability boundary --> Keep original call path: Not applicable
    Check capability boundary --> Handle through a compatible implementation: Applicable
    Handle through a compatible implementation --> [*]
    Keep original call path --> [*]
```

"Keep original call path" in the diagram does not mean that all inapplicable cases share the same alternative logic. It only means that this decision does not authorize callers to continue assuming URL state. What a call site actually does next should be determined by its own existing business logic path; this page does not introduce a unified fallback scheme for containers or Spring.

## How to use the old path

If you still need to look back at the history, you can start with `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/util/ClassUtils.java`. When reading it, first look at its local declarations and immediate neighbors visible in the current revision, then follow the actual references to identify the call sites. Do not use imports of `Introspector`, `Array`, or `Constructor` to infer URL classpath capabilities, and do not treat the file as a public boundary just because it is in a Spring utility package.

LPR-201 serves only as navigation: it preserves the clue that the old call saved the capability result, along with the task of adding back how the call is made and the result the user sees. The interface names on the card can help with searches, but do not replace this page's explanation of the boundary. Once you find the call site, check whether it is querying a capability or has already bypassed the check and is manipulating internal state directly.

DOC-12 is an adjacent record on container transformer ownership. You can read on if you need to understand transformations of StandardWrapper or other container classes; if you are only determining whether a class loader can participate in URL classpath operations, you should not substitute the discussion of container transformers for this page's conclusion.

## Adjacent issues that have not yet been split off

An inventory organized by call site has still not been completed. The existing material only states that legacy calls retain capability results, and does not provide a complete catalog of every consumption point, every kind of not-applicable result, or every layer of loader relationships. This gap should not be papered over with a generic type check.

Another issue is that, although the boundary between the caller side and the implementation side is now clear, legacy notes may still contain wording such as "a capability check allows internal state to be replaced directly". When encountering such wording, treat it as outdated shorthand in accordance with the current decision on this page: the check determines whether to enter the compatibility implementation, not whether callers are free to handle internal UCP themselves.

If a subsequent review finds that a call does not need any URL-type path operations at all, it should not add a capability check just to comply with this decision. The boundary only covers calls that need this type of operation. Conversely, if a call does depend on URL-type paths but does not go through the public surface, restoring the check should take priority over adding another special case based on the type name.

## Appendix: Legacy Examples and Wording

### Legacy Example One: Determining Object Ownership from a File Path

A common formulation in the early notes was "The problem is in `ClassUtils.java`, so handle it from here". This statement remains useful for locating the problem: it can take readers to the place where earlier troubleshooting stopped. It is not valid for determining ownership: a source path is not a runtime object graph, nor is it proof of call relationships.

This legacy example is retained because it remains a starting point for much of the subsequent reading. The right addition is not to remove the path, but to qualify it: after following the path to read the code, you still need to determine the relationship between the caller and the capability implementation based on actual references.

### Legacy Example Two: Treating URL State as a Shared Premise

The legacy example treated the class loader and URL state as nearly equivalent concepts, and therefore tended to try internal handling first, then stop at the point of failure. This example no longer applies to the current version. It omitted the fact that non-applicability is itself a result that should be expressed, not an alias for an exception branch.

This example is now retained to help identify legacy wording. New code should not copy its sequence; it should first go through the public capability boundary, then decide whether to enter the compatibility implementation.

### Early Reminders That Can Still Be Kept

The original reminder, "do not treat every loader as the same", is still valid, but its specific implications were not made clear at the time. It has now been narrowed down to three things: the public capability surface, caller-side preconditions, and the scope of implementation-side operations. The value of the old record lies in reminding us: the issue has never been just whether a particular field can be accessed, but whether the caller has grounds to require it to exist.

First, split the problem by ownership. The bytecode-operation trail in the investigation so far leads to `CtBehavior`, but this area sits near both generic behavior handling and container adaptation; this entry point alone cannot determine who should own the Tomcat changes.

Three tentative options:

- Put container adjustments in the generic bytecode behavior layer, with callers passing only the target class;
- Keep a separate transformation point for Tomcat, with the generic layer providing only the manipulation capabilities;
- Add no new transformation, and handle the differences through container-side configuration.

# Tomcat Transformer Ownership Proposal

This proposal initially tried to find a single home for the changes near `CtBehavior`. That approach was convenient: bytecode operations were kept together, and subsequent calls were easy to trace back through the same class. But it did not answer which component interprets container behavior. A generic behavior object's ability to participate in a modification does not mean it should own Tomcat compatibility semantics.

The conclusion from the last review still stands: `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/javassist/CtBehavior.java` is the entry point for continuing to inspect neighboring bytecode-related code. The file's `AccessFlag`, `AnnotationsAttribute`, and `AttributeInfo` show that this area is close to shared operations, but that is not enough to justify pushing container-class rules into the shared layer. Putting the patch there would make readers see the generic mechanism first, then guess from the call relationships which part is Tomcat-specific logic. That is precisely the ownership arrangement this round aims to avoid.

## Retained Earlier Options

Previous option A: have the generic behavior layer accept the target class, with the caller supplying container conditions. Its advantage is fewer places to change, and the initial draft estimated the work on that basis. We are not adopting it. Once the caller passes in conditions, container versions, initialization parameters, and ordinary bytecode processing share the same extension point; when non-Tomcat classes are encountered later, the code structure makes it hard to tell whether those conditions should still apply.

Previous option C: do not transform container classes; only adjust external configuration. This approach has not been shown to work, nor has it been formally rejected. It cannot replace this proposal at this stage, because the discussion concerns behavior visible on the container classes themselves, not a set of defaults that can be moved entirely into configuration. We are retaining it as an explicit fallback if the independent transformation point cannot be narrowed down, not as a parallel entry point for the current implementation.

The extra classpath and legacy repository issue is not included here. That work concerns ordering constraints in the old class loader; even if both appear near Tomcat initialization, that does not justify making repository decisions an incidental responsibility of the transformer.

## Approach Adopted for This Round

Adopt a separate container transformation surface, and limit the review to container behavior actually interpreted by that transformer. The requirements at this stage are:

The Tomcat bytecode compatibility surface is org.hotswap.agent.plugin.tomcat.WebappLoaderTransformer and its patchStandardWrapper entry point, which changes only the container behavior explicitly owned by that transformer.

This definition establishes ownership; it does not group all Tomcat-related adjustments under one name. When reviewing the implementation, first ask whether the change affects that container behavior. If the only answer is "the shared bytecode layer can do it too," that is not grounds for broadening the patch. `patchStandardWrapper` should serve as the inspection entry point for checking the specific changes around `StandardWrapper`, not as a jumping-off point to other container objects.

Candidate changes must also meet two constraints. First, when invoking generic bytecode capabilities, do not push Tomcat-specific logic back into shared objects; the shared objects remain utilities used by the transformer. Second, the patch's effect should be understandable from the container object alone. For initialization parameters, for example, `development` can serve as a review sample: the task is to confirm whether this container behavior belongs at that transformation point, not to change unrelated parameters along the way.

## Trial Scope and Stop Conditions

The trial covers only the independent transformation point and its direct modifications to container objects. The inspection order is: first locate the target container class, then check whether the patch entry point expresses only conditions for that class, and finally return to the shared bytecode layer to confirm that no Tomcat branches have been added. This order is a little slower than tracing outward from `CtBehavior`, but it can expose ownership drift earlier in review.

Withdraw this trial if any of the following occurs:

- The patch has to store container-specific state in the shared behavior layer;
- Satisfying one container sample affects classes that do not belong to this transformer;
- The patch requires the old repository ordering logic as a prerequisite.

After withdrawal, return to an undecided state; do not automatically activate previous option A. First separate the container behavior from the old class-loader path again, then decide whether the configuration option merits independent validation.

Only two items still need to be filled in: the minimal set of target container classes, and whether a real call dependency exists between legacy repository handling and this transformation surface. The former determines the trial's inspection scope; the latter remains part of the separate legacy-path issue.

# Tomcat Legacy Repository Troubleshooting Tree

The issue observed in the field wasn't the class lookup failure itself, but that even after the extra classpath had been passed to the container, the legacy WebappClassLoader still used its original lookup order. The initial assumption was that as long as the additional entry existed, the container would eventually include it in its search scope; lookup order wasn't called out separately at the time.

Follow the branches below first; don't start by changing the resource resolver.

```text
Extra classpath not taking effect
|
+-- Entry never reached the legacy loader
|   `-- Stop at container initialization and check the object type first
|
+-- Entry reached the loader, but the class still comes from the old location
|   `-- Check where the legacy repositories are stored and their write order
|
`-- Not a legacy loader
    `-- This note doesn't apply; follow the path for the relevant container
```

The legacy repository here is the repository array retained by the loader, not a regular resource directory. Early investigations in the field conflated the two, so troubleshooting focused only on whether the path existed. If the symptom is that a class with the same name still comes from the original location, you should focus first on the first visible position in the array rather than repeatedly checking whether the file has been written to disk.

The nearby entry point recorded for reference is at `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. This file was used as a starting point for reading the code at the time: its package name is `org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.path`, and `File`, `IOException`, and `InvocationHandler` appear near the file header. It can help trace the path handling mentioned in the old notes, but that does not establish that it is responsible for container loading.

Operational note: If all you have is the path-handling result, just record "entry is visible"; don't write "the legacy loader is already using it." The latter requires seeing the array stored by the legacy loader.

# Tomcat Legacy Repository Troubleshooting Tree

Initially, this page treated "whether the additional classpath is visible" and "whether the additional classpath is searched first" as the same question. On review, they need to be separated: the first is whether the entry reaches the legacy loader; the second is its position in the legacy repository. The original wording is retained below because people on call still use this page to find the entry point.

## Old note: Check the path first

> As long as the added entry exists, the container will eventually include it in the search scope.

This sentence is no longer suitable as a troubleshooting conclusion. It still gives some indication of whether the path made it through, but it doesn't say which position the loader uses. When this sentence was used as the check, a common result was that the additional directory was visible, but this still did not explain why the same-named class was not selected.

The old three-step method is retained below:

1. Check whether path handling returns an additional directory.
2. Check whether the container accepts the directory.
3. If the directory exists, assume that the load order is fine.

Step 3 is deprecated. The directory's existence cannot prove its position, nor can it prove that the legacy repository won't hit the original position first when reading it.

## On-call margin note

Later, a short note was left on the troubleshooting sheet:

> "Stop asking whether it was added; ask which position it has."

This is closer to the symptom than the old three-step method. It doesn't identify the write point or distinguish between container versions, so it can only serve as a field reminder. When a class is still loaded from the old location, first confirm that this is the legacy WebappClassLoader case, then inspect the array order that stores the additional entries; if the loader type doesn't match, stop following this page.

```text
Class still comes from old location
|
+-- Runtime object is not legacy WebappClassLoader
|   `-- Stop: don't apply the legacy-repository check
|
+-- It is legacy WebappClassLoader
|   |
|   +-- No additional entry
|   |   `-- Check back whether initialization reached the container object
|   |
|   +-- Additional entry exists, but it comes after the old entry
|   |   `-- Log this as an ordering issue; don't close out with "path exists"
|   |
|   `-- Order cannot be determined
|       `-- Retain the object and the observed symptom; wait for a review that can see the loader state
|
`-- The class source itself cannot be determined
    `-- Don't attribute it to path handling yet
```

## An Incomplete Attempt

A review pass looked for the cause only on the resource-handling side. The entry point for reading was still `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`; the package path at that location and the direct dependencies `File`, `IOException`, and `InvocationHandler` were copied into the margin. The result only confirmed why the old record pointed to path-related objects; it did not establish the container repository's write order.

The mistake at the time was writing "the resource path can be traced from this file" as "this is where Tomcat's additional classpath is determined." Those are not the same. The latter was unsupported; the original conclusion is struck out here.

## Using the Counterexample

The following counterexample is meant to prevent the investigation from ending too early; it does not mean that all containers have been covered: the additional directory is visible, while the same-named class is still resolved from the old location. It narrows the issue from "whether there is a directory" to "which one the legacy loader reads first." If there is no same-named class or the class source cannot be determined, this counterexample cannot be used as a conclusion.

Another easily confused point is an ordinary directory link. Being able to open the ordinary directory doesn't mean that the old binary in production will load from that directory; likewise, being able to see an artifact in the image doesn't mean that the legacy loader's in-memory state has been updated. This page covers only the initialization location of the legacy repository; it does not assign the cause to the container lifecycle or resource resolution.

## Revised Wording After Review

Review raised a specific gap: if the additional entry has in fact entered the array but comes after the original entry, the old three-step method cannot detect it. Therefore, starting with this version, records must include both whether the entry exists and its position relative to the old entry. An on-site record that includes only the first item is not enough to determine whether this page is relevant.

One point from that time remains unresolved: this page does not fill in the call relationship between the path-processing entry point and the container write point. If the only clue available comes from `PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`, treat it as a navigation hint; do not substitute resource-resolution behavior for the legacy loader's state.

## Current Actionable Stop Points

- Not legacy WebappClassLoader: stop; this page does not apply.
- No additional entry visible: go back to the initialization object; the existence of a resource directory cannot substitute for confirmation.
- The entry exists but comes after the old entry: record this as an ordering issue; the old "being added is enough" judgment does not apply.
- The entry is already before the old entry but the symptom is unchanged: stop attributing the issue to the legacy repository; investigate the class source and container lifecycle elsewhere.

This version did not remove all of the old wording. The reason is simple: the old wording still explains why the path was initially checked; it just can no longer serve as the basis for deciding order.

# Tomcat Legacy Repository Troubleshooting Tree

When this page was first recorded, the on-call staff had only a vague symptom to go on: the extra classpath appeared to be present, but the application still behaved as though it was not using it. So the notes started with path handling and only gradually shifted to the repository order in Tomcat's old loader. The old paragraphs and procedures have not all been cleaned up; some entry points still lead people here, but they are retained only for their original purpose.

## The First Guideline from 2023

The original working rule was: "If the appended entry exists, the container will use it for subsequent loading." This statement was too broad. At the time, "exists" sometimes meant that a path object had been created, sometimes that resource handling could return that location, and sometimes merely that an extra directory was visible. These do not describe the same container state.

The original notes described the sequence as:

```text
See the extra directory
  -> Assume the container has accepted the directory
  -> Assume the class with the same name will be obtained from that directory
```

The last step in this chain was later disproved, but that did not make the first two steps meaningless. If the extra directory does not exist, there is still no need to investigate the old repository immediately; it is just that once the directory exists, troubleshooting cannot stop there. The old notes are retained here because, for a time, the only clues available on site were on the path-handling side, and ruling out a missing entry first was reasonable.

The reading entry point retained from that time was `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. The file belongs to package `org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.path`, and its dependencies on `java.io.File`, `java.io.IOException`, and `java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler` are directly visible. Based on this, the early notes called the issue a "path resolution anomaly". In retrospect, that name only describes the neighboring objects observed first; it does not establish actual container ownership.

If all you currently have is a reference to that file, treat it as navigation first: it can help reconstruct why paths were mentioned in the old notes; it cannot answer when the legacy WebappClassLoader stores the extra entry, or which entry comes first when reading. The former practice of treating this file as the place to apply a fix has been discontinued.

## Procedures Left in the Margins

The branches below were transferred from an old on-call paper sheet. The wording has not been fully updated; in particular, "accept" is still too vague.

```text
Extra classpath is not taking effect
|
+-- Path object cannot be obtained
|   `-- Stay on the path-handling side for now, and record the input
|
+-- Path object can be obtained
|   |
|   +-- Container object is not the old WebappClassLoader
|   |   `-- Do not continue down this page
|   |
|   `-- Container object is the old WebappClassLoader
|       `-- The old notes used to end here
|
`-- Class origin cannot be identified
    `-- Do not record directory visibility as successful loading
```

"The old notes used to end here" in this section has been crossed out. It shows where troubleshooting stopped back then: once the old loader was identified, the container was assumed to handle the rest. That assumption did not account for the relative positions of the old entries and the extra entry. The diagram is still retained so that whoever takes over can understand why some old logs contain only a single line saying "directory has arrived", with no array state.

There was another rule of thumb at the time: if nothing was wrong with resource handling, there was no need to look back at the container. That judgment has also been discarded. Resource handling can work normally while the loader still hits the original location first; neither side is a substitute for the other.

## A Review Focused Only on Resource Handling

During the second phase, someone read further through the Java file above, hoping to find the reason the extra classpath was not taking effect in the resource-matching behavior. That review yielded very few useful facts: path-related objects were indeed the entry point for early troubleshooting, and the dependencies visible in the file were also adjacent to local files and reflection proxies.

The facts it did not establish are equally important: this reading did not establish the write point for Tomcat's old repository; it did not confirm that resource resolution results would directly become the first entry in the container repository; nor did it confirm the ordering of any regular directories. Someone later summarized this reading as "the path resolver is responsible for the old loader", but that was not the result of the original review and has been marked in the margin as a misreading.

The failure of this attempt was not a compilation or startup error, but insufficient explanatory power. It could explain why the directory was visible, but not why the class with the same name was still resolved from its original source. Adding more checks on the resource-handling side would only lengthen the troubleshooting checklist, without distinguishing between two cases: the entry never reached the old loader, or it reached the loader but was placed later in the order.

The later notes therefore split the symptom into two questions:

1. Whether the extra entry has appeared in a storage location readable by the legacy loader.
2. If it has appeared, whether it precedes the existing entries.

Only if the answer to the first question is no should you revisit the initialization entry point; only if the answer to the second question is unknown or no should you classify the issue as old repository ordering. If both points have been confirmed and the symptom has not changed, stop using this page; do not continue attributing class origin, container lifecycle, or resource caching to the repository.

## Addendum from 2024: A Class with the Same Name Is a Counterexample, Not a Premise

The counterexample added later was "the extra directory is visible, but the class with the same name still comes from the old location". It disproved the old guideline that "existence means use". The value of this counterexample is that it prompts further investigation of ordering, not that it describes every failure.

Before using it, first confirm that class origin can actually be determined on site. If there is no class with the same name at all, or if only the resource directory is visible and not the actual resolution result, do not enter "the class with the same name is still the old one" in the notes. That would disguise a counterexample used to narrow the scope as an observed symptom.

Likewise, old links in regular directories, permissions on restricted detail pages, artifacts in images, and old binaries in production must be recorded separately. Being able to open a link in a regular directory only shows that the link works; having an artifact in an image only shows that the artifact is in the image; an old binary still present in a production process is another kind of state. None of these alone establishes which repository entry Tomcat's old loader used.

This paragraph was added in particularly firm terms at the time, mainly because several troubleshooting records had directly turned "artifact seen" into "loading has switched". That wording is no longer used. On-site notes should at least distinguish whether what was observed was a path, a repository location, or the actual class origin. When there is no chain of evidence connecting the three, recording "unknown" is better than filling in an inference.

## Retained Old Procedures

The following steps come from an earlier on-call version, and some people still follow them. They have not been deleted, but their stopping condition is no longer valid.

1. Confirm on the path-handling side that the extra directory can be constructed or returned.
2. Confirm that the runtime object belongs to Tomcat's old WebappClassLoader path.
3. After recording that the directory exists, check whether the class is still obtained from the old location.
4. If it is still the old location, return to the container side.

The old version often said "directory attached, waiting for the container to refresh" after step 3. This should no longer be used as a result, because it does not explain the directory's relative position. "Waiting for the container to refresh" also conflates an initialization ordering issue with a lifecycle issue. It is now retained only to help identify wording in historical records.

If someone sees the three Chinese characters meaning "attached" in an old log, they should ask which state it actually means: the path object has been created, the directory is now visible, or an entry is already present in the old loader's array. Without an answer, no further inference should be made.

## Review Excerpts and Revised Guidance

In one review, the issue was condensed into a single sentence:

> "Do not just ask whether it was added; first ask what position it occupies."

This is not a complete design specification, but it clearly identifies the positional relationship missing from the old troubleshooting process. The review comments also required "resource-handling path" and "container repository writes" to be named separately, so readers would not infer from the Java file's path that it owns Tomcat's behavior.

No conclusion was reached at the time on "whether all containers require the same order". This page should not be expanded to answer that question. It deals with the legacy path; if a different loader or a different container object is identified, stop at object identification. Extending the old rule to other classloaders would obscure the boundaries of their own capabilities.

After the review, two mandatory observations were added to the on-call notes: the type of the runtime object, and the extra entry's position relative to the original entries. Earlier records that only said "extra classpath added" can still show that someone looked at the path, but are insufficient to determine the scope of this anomaly.

## Branches Left by an Incident-Style Review

The tree below gives the current troubleshooting order. It does not require running through every branch; enter at a node you can observe. Each stopping point avoids filling in unknowns with conclusions about the container.

```text
Symptom: old classes still appear to be used after adding the extra classpath
|
+-- Cannot identify the running loader
|   `-- Stop: obtain the object type first; do not infer loader state from directory existence
|
+-- Loader is not on the Tomcat legacy path
|   `-- Stop: the old repository branch in this record does not apply
|
+-- Loader is on the Tomcat legacy path
|   |
|   +-- Extra entry is not visible
|   |   `-- Recheck whether initialization reached this loader; this is not yet an ordering conclusion
|   |
|   +-- Extra entry is visible, but its order relative to the old entries cannot be determined
|   |   `-- Record the position as unknown; do not end with "added"
|   |
|   +-- Extra entry comes after the old entries
|   |   `-- Record an ordering anomaly; the old append assumption does not apply
|   |
|   `-- Extra entry is already before the old entries
|       |
|       +-- Class origin can still be confirmed as the old location
|       |   `-- Stop attributing this to the repository, and investigate class origin or lifecycle separately
|       |
|       `-- Class origin cannot be confirmed
|           `-- Retain the current state, without claiming it is resolved
|
`-- Only resource-handling results are visible
    `-- Return to object identification; resource results are not the old repository state
```

The first level of the tree deliberately asks about the loader before asking about any directory. Judgments about the old repository are meaningful only when the object belongs to the corresponding legacy path. Otherwise, even if names, paths, or symptoms are similar, the explanation based on the old array cannot be reused.

The second level separates "entry missing" from "position unknown". A missing entry means the object that would need ordering has not yet been seen; an unknown position means the object has appeared but the on-site evidence is insufficient. Both cases used to be recorded as "waiting for refresh", and this is the conflation that most needs to be avoided.

The third level also contains an easily misused point: an entry coming first does not mean the entire failure has been explained. If the actual class origin still consistently points to the old location, there are conditions beyond this page. Continuing to repeatedly adjust the explanation about the repository will not help at that point; record the currently confirmed order and stop.

## Explanation of Old Terms

On this page, "legacy repository" specifically means the repository array stored by the old WebappClassLoader for its lookups. It does not refer generally to any Maven repository, regular directory list, or resource resolution result. "Extra classpath" means the extra entry passed to that legacy path; its existence, representation, and position in the array must be observed separately.

Early material sometimes called this array repository, and sometimes repository array. Both terms can be retained to avoid misreading old records, but troubleshooting must examine the actual field and position. Do not assume the object has only one entry because the wording uses the singular; nor assume that a new entry naturally comes first because it is an array.

There was another old assumption: Tomcat's path handling would automatically reorder all visible directories. Insufficient evidence for this assumption was retained, and it was not used as an operational premise later. The current approach asks only about the observable storage order in the legacy loader, and does not treat ordinary path enumeration as a substitute.

## Questions Still Left in the Margins

The longstanding presence of the path-handling entry point in this record can now be explained as historical navigation: both the early issue name and the call name led readers to `PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. But the specific call relationship between that entry point and the container write point is not detailed on this page. If someone needs to add that relationship later, they should first obtain the actual references from the same revision, then decide whether to create a separate record; filenames or package names cannot be used to fill in call edges.

Another question that has not been separated out is how to record observations about the container lifecycle, when entry order has been confirmed but class origin still shows the old location, without mixing them back into repository conclusions. For now, this page retains only the stopping condition and does not prescribe a fixed procedure for that question. It shares symptoms with this page, but concerns a different object.

## Currently Applicable Guidance

After the old rules, margin notes, failed resource-side attempt, same-named-class counterexample, and revised review guidance above, the legacy branch retains only one requirement that can be handed off: For the Tomcat 7 legacy path, the public invariant is exactly `Tomcat 7 must prepend the legacy repository array`, and the affected field is named repositories.

This statement constrains only the legacy path of Tomcat 7. During troubleshooting, identify that path first, then read the relative positions of the extra entry and existing entries in `repositories`. Do not rewrite "prepended" as "usually visible after appending", or substitute the ability to obtain a path object for that position. If the array order cannot be observed, the conclusion should stop at "position unknown".

`7` was often treated as an environment label in the old records; here, it identifies the scope of this legacy branch. Even if other container objects also have an extra classpath, this requirement cannot be applied to them merely because their names are similar.

## Old Appendices: Shortcuts That Are No Longer Valid

### Appendix A: Stop Once the Directory Exists

Original text:

> The extra directory has appeared in the resource-handling results, so the container can be considered to look for classes in that directory first.

This paragraph has been discarded. Resource-handling results can only serve as an early observation of the entry; they cannot prove the ordering of the container's old repository. The original text is retained to check why old on-call conclusions lacked array positions.

### Appendix B: Nonempty Means Prepended

Original text:

> If the repository array is nonempty and contains the extra path, there is no need to distinguish the order further.

This paragraph was later disproved by a counterexample. Whether the array is nonempty and whether the extra entry comes first are separate matters. If the old on-site record contains only "nonempty", it still shows that someone examined the container object at the time; but it cannot be used to determine where a class with the same name should be obtained from.

### Appendix C: The Path File as the Only Entry Point

Original text:

> Start investigating all related issues from the resource-matching file.

This was a convenient reading habit at the time, not a conclusion about container ownership. You can still start from that file to find old notes, but once the issue reaches the legacy loader, the focus should shift to the object and array order.

# History of Boot Property Requirements

This page did not originally start from a definite implementation point. In the wrap-up materials for 2026.3 Compatibility Train, the following four names appeared together, making it easy to assume that they naturally belonged to the same Boot refresh chain: Boot listener factory scope, reloadable property-source callback, Boot replacement-state publication, writable Boot loader output. The approach ultimately retained was to keep the four items side by side, but not treat that parallel listing as a shared boundary.

Early records contained only one tentative decision: "Check by factory first." It addressed the listener's scope issue. At that time, there were two ways to frame it. Reusing the existing listener's shared scope would involve few changes, and the old entry point would not need to move; narrowing it according to the actual binding of BeanFactory would explain why events should not consume one another when multiple factories coexist, but first required confirming the binding relationship and event ownership. The record ultimately retained the second as a verification direction, without writing it down as an established public rule. People later continued to use "shared scope" to refer to this, so the sentence remains in the history; it is only an early working hypothesis.

The discussion of property-source was initially mixed together as well. Some people recorded simply rereading a value after a file change as "the property source has been refreshed." This can show the result of one read, but cannot show who initiated the change action. The two options compared were: read the new value directly at the existing read location, or have the property source install a reload callback first, then have the change action publish subsequent state. Direct reading has little impact on existing callers, but the callback might not be part of the event chain at all; the callback option has clearer boundaries, at the cost of having to confirm whether it can still be installed after the property source is created and which object holds it at installation time.

Therefore, the choice left at the time was to continue tracing the callback installation point and the post-refresh read point, and not assume that all PropertySource were reloadable. This decision did not endorse any coverage scope, nor prove that any user entry point was already working. It only separated "being able to read the new value" from "having a refresh path that can be triggered again" as two different things.

Older records for replacement-state publication were more optimistic than the current wording. They once said "call Fang Ke after replacement is complete, as can be seen," but did not specify whether the visible content was in the old reference or was a new object obtained on the next read. The options on the table during review were: one, hide the replacement behind the existing read interface, allowing callers to continue holding the old reference; two, publish the replacement mapping state and require callers to read it again. The first is gentler on old code, but may cause long-held references to continue pointing to old state; the second makes changes easier to observe, but requires determining which callers retain the object. The history retained the requirement represented by the second direction: the published state must be readable again by callers. Object shape and compatibility cost were not settled in these two versions.

writable Boot loader output was also not folded into the listener or property-source. The comparison here was not whether the name "output" existed, but three concrete questions: who holds the output, when writing is allowed, and who continues to read it after it is written. Output generated only during initialization cannot explain later refreshes; allowing writes without a stable holder also cannot show that the result will persist. The record decided to keep it as a separate verification item, to avoid substituting inferences from the other three items for the actual write path.

A simple diagram was once added in the middle of the page to show the split at the time:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Four items recorded separately" as Split
    state "Boot listener factory scope" as Factory
    state "reloadable property-source callback" as Callback
    state "Boot replacement-state publication" as Replacement
    state "writable Boot loader output" as Loader

    [*] --> Split
    Split --> Factory
    Split --> Callback
```

# Raw Resource Lookup Compatibility Workflow

This page originally dealt with migrating verification records, not an implementation refactor. Early investigation treated primitive resource as a form of an ordinary resource name, so when old records were moved to new entries, the only judgment retained was "the first result obtained can continue to be used." That judgment remained here afterward, and many notes in old batches were written on that basis; do not reinterpret those notes as meaning that the lookup order had already been confirmed.

## Legacy Migration Convention

At the time, when compatibility verification was migrated from generic resource records to primitive resource entries, the convention was retained that the first resource obtained was the usable resource. Priority here was treated only as record order; it did not independently change the lookup decision.

During migration, first preserve the resource form supplied by the caller, then copy the original generic verification item under the primitive resource entry. As long as both entries produce the same first result, follow the old record; there was no need to create a separate path for the primitive form.

```text
Old record: generic resource record -> first result -> archive

After migration: primitive resource entry -> still use the first result -> archive
```

To restore the old path, remove the newly created primitive resource verification item and return to the generic resource record. This avoids different conclusions for the same caller appearing in two records.

What remains undecided is whether cases where the resource name is the same but the representation differs should also use the first result. Old records handled them without distinguishing them.

## Later Review Addendum

The follow-up review did not support treating the "first result" directly as proof of precedence. The issue lies in the representation used for resource lookup, not simply in having one more record: even when generic resource entries and primitive resource entries have similar names, it may be necessary to inspect separately what is actually passed to the parser at the entry point. The old workflow did not preserve this layer, so it can show how the records were migrated then, but it cannot substitute for the caller's result.

The code entry point currently available for tracing is `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. That location is part of `org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.path`; the file header shows `java.io.File`, `java.io.IOException`, and `java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler`. These adjacent objects once led people to assume that resource forms would only be merged at the same layer; during review, priority should no longer be inferred from the import list.

Migration records should store two things separately: the raw resource form passed by the caller, and the entry point actually used by that caller. Do not delete the original generic resource entry, because old batches are still reviewed against it; the new entry should not merely say "consistent with the generic resource." If both yield the same result, record only the fact that they match; do not add a priority rationale based on it.

The recommended order for handling the outstanding verification items is:

1. Find entries in old batches that only say "first result"; retain the original wording and flag that they did not distinguish primitive resource.
2. Under the same caller, re-record the resource form and entry point. Record the version and result observed in that instance; do not carry over conclusions from elsewhere.
3. Migrate an old entry into the new primitive resource verification item only when both the raw form and entry point can be matched; leave entries that do not match in the old records.
4. When the old convention needs to be restored, restore the record-keeping method: remove the newly added distinction note and use the generic resource entry as the basis again. Do not infer from this that runtime has returned to any particular lookup order.

Compared with the old workflow, this approach adds one step, but it does not provide a new unified precedence conclusion. The material currently supports only the following: a primitive resource can no longer be verified solely from the first result of the generic resource entry. The ordering of the two entry points in a specific version still needs to be confirmed in the specific caller.

LPR-207 retains the live entry points where this wording is still in use. When tracing back, first verify the caller's actual version, then inspect the entry point and current result; do not first use the old conclusion on this page to filter out samples with inconsistent results.

## Misleading Point Retained

The arrows in the old diagram are easy to read as runtime order:

```text
Generic resource record -> first result -> primitive resource record
```

That sequence actually represents only the registration order at the time. The diagram is unchanged so references from old batches still line up; the text next to it no longer supports using "the first result is sufficient to confirm precedence" in this way.

One adjacent issue has not been split out: when the caller converts the resource form before entering the parser, should the raw form be recorded on the caller side or on the parser side? Existing records have entries on both sides; they have not been merged yet.
