versions.body:
# Plugin Configuration Ordering Decision Record

When plugin configuration ordering appeared in the 2026.3 Compatibility Train materials, it was initially just a description that needed to be cross-checked later. It came with no ordering rules, did not identify a specific plugin, and did not provide the full name of a loading stage or configuration object. However, the issue name and call name left by the earlier investigation led the reading to `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/javassist/CtClass.java`. This entry was specific enough that it was easy to casually treat the file as the implementation location for the issue.

The draft judgment was: do not let this convenient classification become a long-term conclusion. Quality regression in the Compatibility Train needs to retain unresolved issues, and it also needs to leave later readers the actual code locations where the investigation stopped; these are not the same thing. The former is requirement history, while the latter is a verification path. If the path is first written down as the owner, then when the actual call is added later, the material will first require readers to overturn a classification that had no basis.

## What the Old Entry Left Behind

There is not much local code information that can be clearly preserved at present. The path is under the javassist package at `hotswap-agent-core`, and the package name is `org.hotswap.agent.javassist`. Near the file header, `java.io.BufferedOutputStream`, `java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream`, and `java.io.DataOutputStream` are visible. These symbols show that the reading began with local declarations in an existing Java module; they do not show that the configuration maintenance point is here, nor do they provide the ordering of configuration items.

There was once a relatively strong working hypothesis here: since both the issue name and call name pointed to CtClass, the ordering behavior might be determined on the CtClass side. This hypothesis was not retained as a conclusion. The counterexample is not another piece of contradictory code, but a gap in the existing material itself: it can explain why the file should be opened, but it cannot connect any object, call, or output in the file with plugin configuration ordering. The file name, module name, and imports look like a single line when placed together, but they are not yet a call chain.

Therefore, CtClass was not deleted from the record. Deleting it would lose the location where the earlier investigation actually stopped; retaining it still cannot turn it into an alias for configuration ordering. The "entry" here means only that the next reading can start from this path. It does not mean that the file is responsible for ordering, that it determines the final order, or that the I/O adjacency within it is configuration serialization or registration logic.

## The Choices on the Table at the Time

The focus of this decision was not to fill in the missing relationship with a plausible story, but to decide how strongly the existing material should be preserved.

| Handling method | Immediate convenience | Reason for not adopting or adopting it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mark CtClass as owning the sorting implementation | The regression item can be attached directly to a file | The issue name and call name only show that the earlier investigation reached this location; they do not show that the implementation is owned here |
| Infer the configuration-processing chain from the import list | The document would look coherent, and it would be easy to write a longer code explanation | The three I/O types only describe visible adjacency; they cannot establish configuration order, registration timing, or call direction |
| Treat the path as a historical entry and retain the ordering issue separately | The old clue is not lost, and the implementation scope is not fixed prematurely | References still need to be added later, but this avoids bringing speculation into the regression classification |
| Record nothing and wait for complete implementation clues | The current uncertainty would not be left behind | Next time, there would only be an isolated phrase again, and both the old entry and the concerns at the time would disappear |

The risk of the first approach is not that CtClass cannot be read, but that it changes the reading order. Readers will first accept that "ordering is implemented here," and then select the fragments that support this judgment. Even if the actual configuration maintenance point is later found elsewhere, the existing regression description may continue to be organized around the wrong file. Compatibility issues are often missed not because a directory entry is missing, but because an entry was incorrectly elevated to the sole owner very early on.

The second approach is more subtle. `BufferedOutputStream`, `ByteArrayOutputStream`, and `DataOutputStream` are specific names, and writing them in the same paragraph easily creates an imagined "output—configuration—ordering" chain. However, the current record provides neither a configuration operation originating from any of these dependencies nor their relationship to plugin loading. Using imports to complete the business semantics would make a local reading trace bear a conclusion it cannot support.

The fourth approach was also rejected. The fact that the ordering rules have not yet been located does not mean that no decision can be made here. At minimum, it is possible to decide that the requirement phrase must not be swallowed by the path; that the old investigation entry must not be treated as the owner; and that new material should add the actual relationship instead of repeatedly explaining why CtClass was once opened. This preserves a place that still needs investigation without reducing the issue to a one-line to-do item containing only a title.

## Decision

The decision is to preserve plugin configuration ordering as an independent Compatibility Train requirement history. `CtClass.java` will be preserved as the verification entry left by the earlier investigation. The current material does not specify an implementation relationship between the two, and it does not list CtClass as the owner of configuration ordering.

This decision has two boundaries. The historical record preserves why the issue was brought near the javassist path at the time: the issue name and call name had both pointed there. Implementation ownership, however, must be supported by another kind of material: at a minimum, it must show where the ordering requirement actually lands in a call or configuration maintenance location. With only the first type of information, the entry can be recorded; only after the latter appears can the ownership judgment be changed. Putting these two layers in the same paragraph saves space, but it makes a verification clue masquerade as a behavioral conclusion.

The decision makes no judgment about whether CtClass is important. It remains a valid reading location in the existing module, and the package name and direct dependencies near the file header can also help locate the code. What is rejected is only the stronger claim: the current local content cannot establish that "configuration ordering is implemented here" or that "this location determines the final order of plugin configuration." This is not a rejection of the file, but a limitation on the strength of the evidence.

The current wording also has a cost. Later review needs to find the reference relationships separately, and quality regression cannot treat the path as the endpoint of an existing check item. By contrast, the cost of incorrectly fixing the owner is higher: changes to the actual configuration maintenance point may be overlooked, while every regression run will again prioritize the same unconfirmed file. The decision is to retain one explicit follow-up check rather than a seemingly convenient false ownership.

## The Old Judgment Retained in the Draft

The statement in the draft that the work "might be handled on the CtClass side" was not quietly changed into the correct answer; it was retained as the working hypothesis at the time. It explains why the subsequent review needed to specifically check the relationship between the file path and the issue phrase. This hypothesis was later narrowed, not because an opposite implementation location was found, but because the review still produced only navigation information and no definite connection from the path to configuration ordering.

The value of the old judgment is that it exposes the way the material was misread at the time. When a file location is specific enough, it is easy to read "start looking here" as "the answer is here." If this history were deleted entirely, later readers would see only a cautious conclusion and would not see why the stronger speculation initially formed. Retaining it also provides a clear comparison point when new material arrives: did it add the actual call, or did it merely add another local adjacency?

What was removed after review was the implicit endorsement of the hypothesis, not the entry itself. The current wording acknowledges only two known facts: the earlier investigation led the reading to CtClass; and the current local declarations are insufficient to confirm its implementation relationship to the ordering behavior. Other explanations, including configuration serialization, output generation, and plugin registration order, have not been written into this record.

## Impact on Quality Regression Materials

The quality regression side can continue searching for plugin configuration ordering, and it can also review the path starting from CtClass. However, the results of that review need to be recorded separately: if it only confirms the package name, file header, or the I/O dependency, the result can only show that the old entry is still openable; finding a reference that connects the ordering requirement to a specific configuration maintenance location is the material that would change this decision.

The goal of the related tasks is to recover the actual call mechanism and the result seen by users. At this stage, the path name should not be used to invent samples in their place. Without a call, it is not possible to state which layer performs the ordering; without a result, a particular loading behavior cannot be written up as an observed compatibility phenomenon. What is retained here is not abstract "evidence to be added," but two concrete relationships that would change the classification.

The same Compatibility Train also has an interface issue concerning transformer registration idempotence, but it should not be used to fill the gap on this page. Both topics are compatibility work, but that does not make them share an implementation location, regression behavior, or responsibility boundary. The ordering issue needs its own call relationship, and the idempotent registration issue should likewise be judged from its own material. Reviewing both in the same regression batch does not mean that their conclusions can be borrowed from each other.

To avoid repeatedly expanding this history in later quality documentation, other materials need only retain the topic name and the historical entry at CtClass. The comparison of approaches, the reasons for rejection, and the current ownership boundary remain here. Once a new call relationship appears, it should be added directly to this decision and the role of the entry reassessed, rather than having each check page write a different explanation independently.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Historical verification entry
    Historical verification entry --> Relationship pending verification: Issue name and call name point to path
    Relationship pending verification --> Retain entry, ownership undetermined: No definite reference currently found
    Retain entry, ownership undetermined --> [*]
```

## Relationships Yet to Be Added

Two things still need to be added: where the actual call maintains plugin configuration ordering; and what result users specifically see after that call completes. Only when both appear together can it be determined whether CtClass represents implementation ownership, an indirect adjacency, or an investigation turning point that is already outdated. Adding only one of them is still insufficient to upgrade the old entry to the owner.

Until then, this decision remains unchanged: retain the path, retain the narrowed working hypothesis, and retain the status that "the ordering issue has not been located by the current material." When this history is reopened, readers will be able to see both why CtClass was suspected at the time and why that suspicion was not written as a long-term conclusion.

# Proposal to Adjust Transformer Registration

This compatibility review starts with transformer registration idempotence. The boundary for duplicate handling is still unresolved: when the same transformer is registered again, should it be blocked at the registration entry point, or allowed through and detected on the transformation side? There are not enough records to settle this directly.

The trial will initially be limited to duplicate registration within a single run, without treating state across different class loaders, different target types, or restarts as the same problem. The preferred approach is to retain a comparable identity before registration occurs; on the second encounter with the same identity, do not schedule the transformation again. This lets us distinguish "the sample was processed again" from actual duplicate registration.

The review currently starts at `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. Older records left this as a starting point for verification; the file contains direct references to `File`, `IOException`, and `InvocationHandler`. Another option is to keep the marker on the transformer itself. This may cover multiple registration sources, but it would leave each transformer to interpret its own duplicate state, making comparison harder. We will not use regression test order alone to avoid a second registration; the same type of problem would remain if the order changed.

For the trial, first find an existing example that reproduces the issue reliably: make the same registration twice in succession, and compare the first and second registration results and the traces of subsequent processing. If the example has to be modified to show a difference, stop there and do not record it as a basis for regression testing.

Open questions: whether the identity needs to include the class loader; whether the marker should be retained after a failure; which component should own deduplication if the entry point is outside the current investigation path. # Transformer Registration Adjustment Proposal

The initial draft framed the issue as "repeated processing," but that wording is too broad. Later, when checking against LPR-210, the phenomenon in the card was that the actual transformer entry point and the sample result were inconsistent, and the to-do item explicitly required finding the shortest real example from the existing regressions and checking whether it could still be processed again. Two things need to be separated first: whether a registration is accepted a second time, and why the sample still appears capable of being processed again after a conversion. The former is what this trial is intended to constrain.

The old record directed verification to `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/path/PathMatchingResourcePatternResolver.java`. This lead remains, but we will no longer use it as the basis for treating resolver as the transformer's registrar. The file header currently shows `package org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.path;`, along with references to `java.io.File`, `java.io.IOException`, and `java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler`; these can only help resume code reading and cannot replace confirmation of the actual call chain.

## The duplicate behavior this trial is meant to suppress

In this document, "registration" means the action of asking the runtime to install a transformer; it is not equivalent to that transformer having already modified a class. The trial is intended to ensure that when the same logical transformer is submitted again, the second submission does not create a new registration state. It does not promise to merge the processing of all classes that merely look similar, nor to join state from before and after a runtime restart.

At present, the proposed candidate components of identity are the logical transformer, its target, and, when necessary, the class-loader boundary. Using the class name alone as the identity is convenient, but when same-named classes exist across class loaders, it can incorrectly collapse two independently processable objects into one. Conversely, if only the object instance is considered, recreating the same registration request may completely evade deduplication. Neither risk can be determined merely from "the same sample looks unchanged."

The minimum semantics of the trial are: within the same runtime window, a second registration confirmed to be for the same logical request must not add a new transformation task; the existing behavior established by the first registration must not disappear because of this check. This definition deliberately leaves concurrency, unloading, and recovery across runtime windows out of scope. They may be related, but the current material does not provide usable examples.

## Candidate locations

**Deduplication at the entry point.** Compare identity after the registration action enters and before it affects subsequent conversion. The advantage is that repeated requests are intercepted in one place, and the regression can directly observe the difference between the first and second requests. The cost is that the actual entry point must first be found; if the current path is merely adjacent to resource resolution, forcing state into it would create a new ownership problem.

**A flag inside the transformer.** Each transformer determines before actual processing whether it has already been registered. This appears to avoid locating the entry point, but the flags would be scattered across multiple implementations. If different transformers interpret "same" differently, the compatibility issue changes from duplicate registration to inconsistent rules. This approach can serve as a fallback if the entry point cannot be unified, but it is not the direction for the first implementation round.

**Avoiding the second request through sample execution order.** This is not a fix. If the sample order, test fixture, or caller changes even slightly, duplicate registration will still occur; moreover, "there was no second call" and "the second call was correctly ignored" will become indistinguishable in the result. Therefore, it is not recommended merely to make a short example pass.

Another approach is to determine directly from the conversion result whether it has already been processed. This can avoid duplicate modification in some situations, but it ties registration state to the bytecode result. For this round's interface review, the cost is too high: a visible result does not show that the registration was not saved twice, and later cleanup or replacement may still have to deal with two copies of the state.

## Re-verify first, then make the smallest change

LPR-210 provides only one clear work entry point: select the shortest real example from the existing regressions, then check whether it can be processed again. During verification, first record the registration requests triggered by the example rather than only checking whether the final sample succeeds. It must be possible to distinguish among these three observations: no second request was issued; a second request was issued but rejected or ignored at the entry point; the second request entered, but the conversion side produced no additional effect. The first two have different implications for interface design, and the third cannot prove registration idempotence.

The tentative verification order is: first trace the registration call site back through the existing example; then confirm the transformer, target, and class-loader information used by the two requests; finally, add the comparison only near the confirmed entry point. If the identity inputs for the two requests are inherently different, they must not be forced to be "the same" merely to manufacture a passing result.

The `InvocationHandler` in the current path is an adjacent point worth watching: if the actual request passes through a proxy or reflection wrapper, identity comparison cannot rely solely on the outer object. This does not require incorporating the proxy structure into the implementation; it only requires checking whether the request is wrapped before deciding to use object identity. `File` and `IOException` likewise should not be treated as registration evidence; they may belong only to the resource-matching process.

Success is not judged by the single criterion of "the second time did not error." A second request that does not error may mean that it was correctly ignored, or it may mean that the duplicate state was still silently accepted. At a minimum, the trial must make the records able to answer: whether the second request reached the registration entry point, whether the entry point identified it as the same logical request, and whether subsequent processing added state that can be processed further. If the existing regression cannot preserve these distinctions, add observation points first, then discuss fixed assertions.

## Out of scope and rollback

This round does not treat similar targets belonging to different transformers as duplicates, nor does it attempt to unify the entire lifecycle of resource resolution, proxy wrapping, and actual class transformation. In particular, do not treat state in the path as a global registry just because the resolver path is adjacent to the issue name. If the actual registration point is elsewhere, the change should move with the entry point.

There are two rollback conditions. First, if the existing processing from the first registration disappears after deduplication, that indicates that the comparison was made too early or that the identity information is incomplete. Second, if two class-loader boundaries that should be independent are merged, that indicates that the identity definition is too narrow. If either occurs, withdraw this deduplication check, retain the verification records, and do not use sample order to conceal the issue.

If entry-point review shows that the duplicate comes from the caller explicitly issuing two requests in the same flow, protection can still be added at the registration layer; however, caller duplication and registration-layer protection must be recorded separately. Otherwise, later looking only at "already deduplicated" would lead us to mistakenly believe that the upstream request has returned to normal.

## Undecided

- Whether identity comparison must include the class loader, or whether it can be naturally isolated by the registration entry point.
- Whether the ignored second request needs to leave a diagnostic trace, to prevent the sample result from masking caller duplication.
- After the shortest real example is found, whether its reprocessing occurs at the registration stage or the conversion stage.
- If the current verification path is not the entry point, which component is responsible for retaining this short-lived state.

Until these items are resolved, do not elevate the trial into a general registration rule.

# Troubleshooting Tree for the Tomcat Disable Lifecycle

This old troubleshooting entry point is still referenced, but it originally focused attention on proxy generation. That was because both the issue name and the call name had led people to `plugin/hotswap-agent-proxy-plugin/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/plugin/proxy/java/ProxyGenerator.java`. On subsequent review, this path could still serve as a checkpoint; it was no longer suitable as the sole explanation for disabled Tomcat lifecycle.

LPR-211 recorded this type of state anomaly and asked the relevant module maintainers to verify the current behavior and the entry points available for further investigation. The card later had a `qa_reproduced` action; that action indicates a need to return to the actual environment for verification and cannot replace records of the processing sequence, where the state changed, or container ownership.

First, break down the "anomaly" into concrete points that can be documented. Do not assume either that Tomcat was not disabled or that a proxy class remained in use after disablement succeeded. First establish three closely related facts: whether the disable operation was entered, the state observed when lifecycle processing ended, and whether the anomaly occurred during processing or in a subsequent call. If any of the three is missing, do not jump to a fix branch.

```text
Abnormal state after Tomcat is disabled
|
+-- No verifiable before-and-after states for the operation itself
|   |
|   +-- Only the caller's abnormal result is visible
|   |   `-- Stop: add the pre-processing state, post-processing state, and triggering sequence.
|   |
|   `-- Entry into the operation is confirmed, but no end state is available
|       `-- Stop at the lifecycle entry point; do not switch to changing proxy generation.
|
+-- Before-and-after processing states are visible
|   |
|   +-- The anomaly occurs before disable processing has finished
|   |   `-- Trace back through the container lifecycle entry point, and record which step changed the state first.
|   |
|   +-- The anomaly appears only after disable processing has finished
|   |   |
|   |   +-- The old records also point to ProxyGenerator
|   |   |   `-- Verify whether proxy generation was actually reached, then decide whether to continue.
|   |   |
|   |   `-- No evidence of proxy generation
|   |       `-- Stay on the container side, without recasting the issue as a proxy-class problem.
|   |
|   `-- The before-and-after states are the same, and only the call results differ
|       `-- Record the specific call location; the existing old records are insufficient to determine that the lifecycle has failed.
|
`-- Reproduction conditions are unstable
    `-- Retain the observed sequence, stop the investigation at the reproduction conditions, and do not adjust the disable path on this basis.
```

## Scope of the Old Entry Point

An early draft treated `ProxyGenerator` as the first stop. This choice is retained here to show where the investigation focused at the time, not to confirm that this class owns the Tomcat lifecycle. The following declarations can be located directly in that file:

- `public class ProxyGenerator {`
- `public static byte[] generateProxyClass(final String name, Class<?>[] interfaces) {`
- `public Void run() {`
- `private byte[] generateClassFile() {`
- `addProxyMethod(function, line 577)`
- `checkReturnTypes(function, line 614)`

Of these, the parameters of `generateProxyClass` are useful for documenting the sources of the class name and interface set when the proxy-generation branch has actually been reached; `run` and `generateClassFile` can be used to confirm whether generation has started. Do not interpret every outcome after Tomcat is disabled as a generation failure just because these entry points exist in the file.

The file header shows standard Java dependencies related to output and files, including `ByteArrayOutputStream`, `DataOutputStream`, and `File`. This can help readers see why the old records pointed to the generation path, but it does not show Tomcat's disable processing itself. At this point in the investigation, treat it as a check of "whether proxy generation is involved," not as a conclusion about ownership of the container lifecycle.

## Procedure in the Actual Environment

**First, ask whether processing actually started.** If the report only says "anomaly after being disabled," add the state before the disabled action was submitted, along with the state observed when the action returned or in subsequent steps. Without these two points, it is impossible to distinguish between the operation never being entered, the operation being interrupted, or reuse by another call after the operation completed. The old records do not contain this sequence, so the old file location cannot be used to fill that gap.

**Next, ask which stage the anomaly falls in.** If the anomaly occurs before disable processing has finished, prioritize retaining the container lifecycle entry point and the state changes at that time. Checking `generateProxyClass` at this point will often yield only a nearby Java generation point and cannot explain why the disable operation did not complete. Unless observations from the actual environment already show that the generation entry point was called, do not treat this function as the next step.

**If disablement has finished.** Only then check the old path. First confirm whether `run` was reached; if not, ProxyGenerator should no longer remain the focus of the investigation. If it was reached, check whether `generateClassFile` continued executing, and record the sources of `generateProxyClass`'s `name` and `interfaces` arguments. Only record branches actually entered here, without guessing the container state from class names.

**If the state is unchanged before and after processing.** This is neither evidence against "disablement succeeded" nor evidence of a proxy-generation anomaly. It only means that the state observations in the current record are insufficient to explain the call result. After retaining the call location and processing sequence, have the relevant module maintainer confirm the lifecycle state definitions; this page does not contain enough material to close this branch with a specific conclusion about the implementation.

**If it cannot be reproduced consistently.** Do not record a single failure to reproduce as recovery. Retain the disabled conditions used at the time, the processing sequence already observed, and whether the old proxy-generation entry point was reached. The next time both the before-and-after processing states and the location of the anomaly can be captured, start again at the root of the tree. This avoids incorrectly recording "did not recur" as "the lifecycle is now normal."

## Previously Ineffective Backtracking Approaches

The old workflow included a shortcut: jumping directly from the issue name to `ProxyGenerator`, then tracing back around `generateProxyClass`. Its value was in quickly confirming whether the proxy-generation code was reachable; it did not indicate when the disabled state changed, nor did it identify the Tomcat lifecycle entry point. After review, this approach belongs only in the "after disable processing has finished, and there are signs of proxy generation" branch.

Another action prone to misjudgment is seeing `run` and immediately recording the anomaly as "generation did not complete." `run` is a function that can be located, but this does not mean it ran during this anomaly, much less that it determines whether the container is disabled. First record the fact that it was reached, then record what happened next with `generateClassFile`; if there is no evidence that it was reached, leaving it blank is more useful than adding a causal attribution.

## Stop Points and Handoff Content

When any of the following occurs, the investigation on this page should go no further:

- Only post-disable symptoms are available, with no before-and-after processing states;
- It can only be shown that the old records point to ProxyGenerator, not that this call entered that class;
- Proxy generation has been entered, but the anomaly still occurs before lifecycle processing has finished;
- The reproduction attempt did not leave a state sequence sufficient for comparison.

At handoff, include only the three items observed in the actual environment: the states before and after the disabled action, whether the anomaly occurred during processing or in a subsequent call, and whether ProxyGenerator's `run` was actually reached. If the generation branch was reached, simply add the sources of `generateProxyClass`'s parameters. Do not treat the path priorities on this old page as the responsibility boundaries of the current implementation.

## Adjacent Issues Retained for Reference

`FieldInfo(type, line 692)` is also easy to come across while browsing the old file, but the existing material does not connect it to disabled Tomcat lifecycle. Unless observations from the actual environment already show that the proxy-generation branch has been entered and this type is involved, do not include it in this investigation path.

LPR-211 remains the navigation entry point for state anomalies. The conclusion retained here is limited: first establish the actual stage of disable processing, then decide whether to investigate proxy generation; the old path can assist with verification, but cannot by itself replace investigation on the lifecycle side.

# History of Spring Cache Requirements

2026.3 Compatibility Train groups CGLIB wrapper reuse, properties refresh scheduling, and Spring metadata cache clearing into the same batch of compatibility issues. The initial draft did not treat them as one implementation change: they all fall within a Spring-related hot-reload context, but the issues were raised differently, and their regression symptoms are not interchangeable.

At the time, the decision was to keep three independent confirmation criteria.

- CGLIB wrapper reuse focuses on whether the wrapper object can still be used through the original path on repeated entry; do not define reuse as a particular fixed caching strategy yet.
- properties refresh scheduling only records that legacy calls still need the refresh result to be retained. The scheduling time, merge method, and trigger source have not been determined.
- Handle Spring metadata cache clearing separately. Seeing one refresh cannot directly show that the metadata cache has been cleared as expected.

The earlier investigation traced from the issue name and call name to `hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/util/ClassUtils.java`. Use this as the lookup entry for now. The file header shows dependencies on `Introspector`, `Array`, and `Constructor`, so the adjacent reflection and class utility code is a suitable place to start.

versions.body:
# History of Spring Cache Requirements

This record initially put the three names on the same line simply because they all entered the 2026.3 Compatibility Train backlog, not because it had been proven that they shared a single reload path. When it was reviewed later, this arrangement instead caused a misreading: seeing CGLIB wrapper reuse, properties refresh scheduling, and Spring metadata cache clearing linked together, readers easily began looking for a common switch, or treating a successful sample for one item as evidence for the other two.

At the time, there was not enough material to support this merger. This same decision record is retained to preserve a narrow tradeoff: delivery cadence can be shared, but problem definitions and verification criteria must not be conflated.

The earliest source entry left was:

`hotswap-agent-core/src/main/java/org/hotswap/agent/util/spring/util/ClassUtils.java`

The old investigation was directed here by the issue name and call name. The file belongs to the `org.hotswap.agent.util.spring.util` package, and its header directly imports `java.beans.Introspector`, `java.lang.reflect.Array`, and `java.lang.reflect.Constructor`. These clues made it a reading entry point for Spring utilities and reflection-adjacent code, but did not pin down the wrapper lifecycle, property refresh scheduling, or metadata cache invalidation location together.

The draft once said, "first consolidate the three issues from ClassUtils." That sentence was not deleted because it explains why someone later opened this file first; however, it no longer indicates processing order. It turned "can start looking here" into "should be solved here."

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Same-batch backlog
    Same-batch backlog --> CGLIB_wrapper_reuse
    Same-batch backlog --> properties_refresh_scheduling
    Same-batch backlog --> Spring_metadata_cache_clearing
    CGLIB_wrapper_reuse --> Independent verification
    properties_refresh_scheduling --> Independent verification
    Spring_metadata_cache_clearing --> Independent verification
```

The diagram only indicates that these three items were split up for independent verification within the same batch backlog. It does not mean that they already have a shared implementation, nor that any one of them is complete.

## Three Approaches Compared at the Time

The first approach was to group all three items under the same Spring reload subproblem, find a common entry point, and modify them together. This approach made scheduling simple and allowed the same round of environment preparation to serve multiple checks. Its problem was not that the three items were entirely unrelated, but that their failure symptoms differed: whether the wrapper was reused, whether the property result was republished at the appropriate time, and whether the cache was actually invalidated each require a different observation point. One branch passing cannot determine the other two branches.

The second approach was to designate the implementation location according to the earliest source path. `ClassUtils.java` had been mentioned by the old investigation and had clear reflection-related dependencies, so it appeared at the time to be a quicker landing point. This approach was not adopted later. Adjacency to the utility class can explain part of the investigation direction, but cannot show where properties refresh scheduling is arranged or define the boundary of Spring metadata cache clearing. If it were written as the sole entry point, the later checks would become circular: modify the entry point first, then use the modified entry point to prove itself.

The third approach was to let the Compatibility Train retain a common regression theme while splitting the three issues into three separate determinations. This approach was adopted. It did not promise a shared implementation, nor did it promise that the three issues would be closed in the same round of changes; it only required that the record not let a successful symptom for one issue replace confirmation of another.

Adopting the third approach does not mean concluding that the three are completely unrelated. The wording in the draft was too close to that meaning, and was understood that way during later reviews. The more accurate old conclusion should be: the connection between the three was not yet concrete enough to design a shared fix on that basis, so checks should not initially be organized around a common attribution.

## The Old Assessment of the Wrapper

The focus of CGLIB wrapper reuse is reuse, not "creating another working wrapper." The draft did not specify where the wrapper was held, its key, or its release conditions, so object identity rules cannot be inferred from this record. In particular, a single successful proxy call cannot be used to claim that subsequent calls reused the same wrapping relationship.

The decision left at the time was narrow: treat the wrapping behavior after repeated entry as part of the compatibility surface, and do not make the number of temporary objects during reload a conclusion. This preserved the original direction of the requirement without hard-coding the implementation as a global cache, Bean-level cache, or class-level cache in the absence of a local sample.

One boundary was unanswered at the time. If wrapper reuse depends on the actual interface class loader of the Spring Bean, the issue is closer to the proxy definition location; if it depends only on the CGLIB generated class, the observation method is different. The existing material contains no call snippet that can distinguish these two cases. The import list of `ClassUtils.java` cannot answer this question either.

The old version abbreviated "wrapper reuse result regression after upgrade" as "the wrapper was not reused." This abbreviation was later considered too strong: it directly treated a regression at the result level as a conclusion about the object lifecycle. The original wording remains near the historical entry because it explains why the investigation once focused on the wrapper creation site; it should no longer be treated as a confirmed attribution.

This record also did not choose to rewrite CGLIB wrapper reuse as a general proxy-cache requirement. What needs to be retained in the Compatibility Train is the behavior of the repeated path, not a prior declaration of which layer must hold the wrapper object long-term. If a clear call relationship appears later, first determine whether initial creation, repeated entry, and re-entry after reload belong to the same path, and then discuss the unit of reuse.

## The Boundary of properties refresh scheduling

The starting point for the properties refresh scheduling record is that legacy calls need to retain the result of properties refresh. "Retaining the result" does not automatically define scheduling semantics. It cannot by itself say whether the refresh should run immediately, be delayed, be coalesced, or be scheduled by which resource-change entry point.

The draft once tended to treat "the legacy call can still see the result" as evidence that scheduling was correct. This was too broad a judgment. The call result only shows that some visible state was not completely lost; it cannot distinguish whether the refresh was scheduled within the correct window. If multiple resource changes fall within the same window, the final state may look correct while masking an intermediate refresh that was not scheduled.

Therefore, the decision for this item is to record result retention separately from scheduling. Within the Compatibility Train, a single final value should not yet substitute for scheduling confirmation, and queues, delays, or coalescing mechanisms that have not been observed should not be written as facts. If a local call site becomes available later, first state whether it triggers a resource change, property publication, or a read; only after this distinction is clear is it appropriate to discuss ordering.

This item and wrapper reuse can appear in the same regression round, but they cannot share the same judgment that "it still works after reload." The former asks whether property refresh was scheduled and left a result visible to the legacy call; the latter asks whether the wrapping relationship is preserved during reuse. Both may appear as continued executability after reload, but their actual meanings are different.

The draft also contained an incomplete judgment: as long as the legacy call ultimately reads the updated property, the intermediate scheduling process can temporarily be ignored. This was suitable for scheduling triage at the time, but not as a long-term conclusion. It does not distinguish between "the final state was not lost" and "every resource change received scheduling." The old record retains this gap because there was not yet enough local call material to separate the two.

## Scope of metadata cache handling

Spring metadata cache clearing was listed separately because, in prose, "cache clearing" can easily lose sight of the object involved. The draft only described it as a confirmation item for an existing check; it did not specify the particular cache instance, its holder, or the rebuild path. This was the boundary of the information known at the time and should not be turned into a generalized Spring caching strategy in the supplement.

The judgment adopted here is equally conservative: clearing can be recorded as confirmed only when the check can connect the refreshed behavior to a definite metadata cache state. A class load, a Bean creation, or a successful configuration read is insufficient on its own to cover this judgment. These may be investigation observations, but they are not proof that the cache was cleared.

One early direction was to first inspect behavior near the reflection utility. `Introspector`, `Array`, and `Constructor` meant that this direction was not entirely unfounded at the time, especially when identifying types or constructor adjacency. However, this was only a reading entry point and did not prove that the Spring metadata cache was held or cleared by that utility class. Later, the cache responsibility should not be assigned to `ClassUtils.java` merely because this entry point is convenient.

This distinction was once hidden by scheduling language. The schedule can say "confirm all three together," but the actual record must ask separately: whether repeated wrapping still reuses the original relationship, whether property refresh has been scheduled, and whether the metadata cache has an identifiable invalidation. Compressing the three questions into one "Spring reload is normal" will make the hardest-to-identify cache issue disappear first.

## Shared Scheduling, Separate Conclusions

The Compatibility Train still places all three items under the same regression theme because they all expose compatibility issues during Spring-related updates, and the same round of preparation may cover multiple entry points. "Shared" here refers only to work organization, not to the implementation mechanism.

| Item | Judgment retained at the time | Content not decided at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CGLIB wrapper reuse | The repeated path still requires a separate check | Whether the wrapper is held by a fixed cache or fixed scope |
| properties refresh scheduling | The refresh result of the legacy call must not be lost | Scheduling time, trigger source, and coalescing rules |
| Spring metadata cache clearing | Clearing requires independent confirmation | Whether any successful refresh can represent that the cache was cleared |

This table adds the distinction missing from the draft. The second column contains the requirements that were decided to be retained at the time; the third contains implementation conclusions that were not determined. When the two columns were not separated, "needs checking" was often read as "already located."

Some readers may extend the proxy issues from the same batch to JDK proxy loader selection or application loader propagation. Those two directions are outside the decision scope of this page. They may appear in Compatibility Train materials alongside this page, but should not be written into the conclusion for CGLIB wrapper reuse. If an investigation touches both proxy and class-loader conditions, the proxy type and loader condition should still be recorded separately.

## Outstanding Items Retained

- The unit of reuse for wrapper reuse has not been specified: it may be a single proxy creation, a particular Bean, or a narrower call relationship.
- There is not yet enough material to distinguish the trigger, scheduling, and publication for properties refresh scheduling.
- metadata cache clearing has not been reduced to a cache boundary that can be named; an existing check item cannot replace this identification.
- `ClassUtils.java` is an old navigation entry; whether it participates in any actual path still depends on the call references in the revision at the time.

Therefore, the valid decision in this record remains to split confirmation rather than designate an implementation. The old statement about "consolidating everything at a single entry point" no longer applies; the old entry point and comparison process remain to explain why these three terms have long appeared together in Compatibility Train materials.

title: Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Record

versions.body:
# Quality Signal Cache Decision Record

plugin · Quality Signal Board left two kinds of material at the current revision: a cache for later comparison, and the original state retained when failure samples were captured. Both are available, but neither can substitute for the other in the same assessment. The disagreement centers on whether to continue using the existing state when review begins or rebuild the environment first.

## Approaches considered

The first approach keeps the current revision. The cache remains the reference for regression tiering, while the original state stays with the failure samples for reference when attributing unstable signals. The trade-off is that the cache does not automatically establish all the conditions under which a sample was produced. Anyone reading the record still needs to refer back to the original state to make that judgment.

The other approach is to rebuild the environment first, then collect a new set of materials. This proposal aims to eliminate questions the old cache might raise, but it would also change the relationship between the existing environment and the current revision. Even if the results then differed, it would be hard to tell whether the difference came from the cache, the original state, or the rebuild itself.

## Decision

Keep the current revision. Do not make rebuilding the environment a prerequisite for this decision. Keep the cache as the entry point for comparisons in the Quality Signals Dashboard; keep the original state as context for failure samples. Regression tiering may reference the cache, but the original state must not be deleted or overwritten just because the cache is still available.

This decision covers only how the existing materials are preserved and the order in which they are used. It does not extend to a blanket conclusion about all tests. The existing records support this much: continuing comparisons under the same revision makes it easier to see what the cache contents and the original state each preserved; rebuilding the environment would mix new conditions into the differences we are trying to identify.

## Objections on record

One objection is that later readers may treat the cache as the complete original state and stop looking at the failure samples. This is a valid concern, so the original state must be kept alongside the cache, rather than retaining only the classified results. Another concern is that the original state is too fragmented to provide a stable entry point for regression tiering. The response is not to delete the originals, but to let the cache continue serving as the entry point.

Rebuilding the environment is not the default action when backing out, either. If this decision no longer applies, first stop using the cache as a substitute for the original state and return to checking failure samples against the original state. Keep the records for the current revision so that backing out does not erase the basis for the comparisons made at the time.

Two unresolved items remain in the record: the active callers of `property publication`, and whether backing out should only restore the old entry point. They will affect subsequent usage, but are not enough to overturn the decision to keep the current revision first.

The materials are located at `docs/adj-plugin/decisions/plugin-quality-signal-cache-vs-live-source-tradeoff.md`. plugin · Quality Signal Board continues to maintain the attachments; this record preserves the choice between the cache and the original state, and the limits of that choice.

| Waiting phase | The CI queue was stuck, and local results were no longer used for assessment | During this period, local green results were not documented as proof of recovery |
| Interface checks | The chronological order of events, caller integration-testing records, and index timestamps was inverted | LPRB-011 moved into interface checks, with unexplained time differences listed separately |
| Retracing the entry path | Real consumers needed to reach the original records from the directory or report | LPRB-009 retained the verification task for the first broken-link location |
| Cleaning up explanations | The navigation entry point for the current revision could be retained, but explanations without a source needed to be removed | LPRB-013 addressed only the explanatory text, without declaring the root cause settled |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Caller enters from directory or report] --> B[Current revision entry point]
    B --> C{Records distinguish revisions}
    C -- No --> D[Preserve original entry point and samples]
    D --> E[Check old relationships and index timing]
    E --> F{User path restored}
    F -- Yes --> G[Record recovery time]
    F -- No --> H[Continue retaining broken-link location]
```

Here, "user path restored" means only that consumers can continue through the original entry point to completion, not that the two records have been merged or that factory scope has been explained. The first version conflated recovery and root cause too closely; the second version records them separately: the former is the observed state, while the latter remains open.

## Two Assessments That Are Easy to Confuse

**Whether the old relationships were withdrawn.** The check recorded in LPRB-007 was to replay the exit action and see whether the old edges actually disappeared. A later public explanation attributed that round of expiration actions to the hot cache. This can explain why the display remained unstable after withdrawal, but it cannot, on its own, prove that the hot cache created the two versions of the records, nor can it replace checking the actual relationships at the entry point.

**Whether the index timestamps were correct.** The issue in LPRB-011 was an inversion in the chronological order of events, caller integration-testing objects, and index timestamps. The same shift log showed different expiration actions on the two sides, indicating that this part can no longer be summarized as "one current state". Even after the interface checks are complete, unexplained time differences still need to be retained, rather than choosing one side to overwrite the other.

The differences in configuration identity saved at the outset remain valuable clues, but are not a root-cause conclusion. They only show that the material provided by the entry point differed from the old records. In contrast, classloader ownership showed no anomalies in the initial comparison; this result narrowed the scope of suspicion at the time, but does not imply that all the other layers were normal.

LPRB-005 completed scope confirmation first, and only then became blocked because the CI queue had stalled. The fact that local results were no longer used does not mean they were necessarily wrong, only that they were not used to override the observed state at the entry point. With this distinction added, the recovery assessment has a clear boundary: only the results real consumers obtain by following the original entry point are recorded as the path state.

Samples of the old relationships were attached before the withdrawal checks, and the interface checks later entered review. When the board was backfilled, the commit to the caller integration-testing core module had already occurred before the board sync, so the relationships between records cannot simply be inferred from the order in which they appeared on the board. This supplementary note explains why the index-order inversion cannot yet be reduced to a single timing issue, but does not explain why the two revisions shared the current entry point.

## Impact and Stopping Points

The affected consumers are those who navigate from the current revision to the integration-testing records. If, after entering from the directory or report, the first broken-link location is still before the entry point, first write that location back to LPRB-009; if the entry point is accessible but displays explanations without a source, retain the navigation and remove the explanatory text according to LPRB-013. Do not combine these two symptoms into a single "entry-point anomaly".

While the CI queue was blocked, local results were not used further downstream; therefore, those results are excluded from the recovery assessment. The original secondhand account, which contained only screenshots, also did not retain enough context and cannot explain why the other path worked normally. The second version no longer cites that account as a basis for assessment.

Questions that remain unanswered:

- Why factory scope changed between the two records;
- Whether, after the old relationships are replayed, the entry point still treats the other revision as the current record;
- Whether the inversion in index timing is a record-ordering issue or an entry-point selection issue;
- Whether the restored user path covers all adopters.

This page still retains the early assessment that "the old index had not been refreshed", to help explain why the entry point was examined first at the time; it is no longer sufficient to explain the full anomaly. Subsequent checks will continue separately for the entry point, old relationships, and index timing, without substituting one green result for confirmation in all three areas.

# Postmortem on unmerged caller integration testing records

This postmortem preserves an account of a record-merging anomaly that was never fully resolved. The caller integration testing entry point once placed two revisions under the same "current revision"; when consumers accessed it through that entry point, they saw a configuration identity that differed from the one in the old record, but did not have enough information to tell which version they were reading.

The initial response was to save the material visible at the entry point and stop retrying. The goal at that point was narrow: prevent subsequent attempts from overwriting the original two sets of relationships again. Later, the user path recovered, and the wrapper lifecycle also recovered; but these two recovered states did not explain why factory scope had changed, much less prove that the entry point had correctly merged the two versions of the record.

The original explanation from the first version is retained here: **"The old index was not refreshed."** It seemed reasonable at the time, because the entry point had indeed retained the old relationships. Later verification showed that this statement alone could not explain the difference in configuration identity, the reversed order of indexing times, and the inconsistent expiration actions in the same shift record. It was the starting point during the incident, not a complete account of the cause as currently understood.

## The first anomaly observed

The first anomaly was not a clearly anomalous output, but ambiguity in the entry point's semantics. The entry point was still labeled as the current revision, yet consumers received a configuration identity different from the one in the old record. Because the two revisions shared the same entry point, the page alone could not show whether the new record had overwritten the old record, or whether the old relationships still kept both sets of material side by side at the current location.

Initially, this behavior was considered together with the wrapper lifecycle. During later checks, the wrapper lifecycle could be restored, so some were inclined to attribute the issue to a brief delay in lifecycle recovery. That assessment was later withdrawn: lifecycle recovery only describes a recovered state and cannot establish that the entry point relationships, indexing order, or scope of adoption are already normal.

factory scope was another change that was not adequately explained at the time. It differed between the old record and the material visible at the entry point, but there were not enough records to link this change to a particular revision, a specific indexing operation, or a particular exit action. This issue has persisted from the first version to the present and remains an unknown.

## Incident notes and later additions

| Phase | What could be confirmed | Action taken at the time | Remaining limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial entry-point divergence | Two revisions shared the current entry point, and the configuration identity differed from that in the old records | Saved the entry-point version and original input | It was not confirmed which revision the entry point should select |
| Initial comparison | No anomalies were observed in classloader ownership | Narrowed the focus by moving away from class-loading relationships | This comparison cannot cover the index or old relationships |
| Retries paused | Further attempts might overwrite the incident state | Stopped looking for results by repeatedly refreshing the entry point | Branches outside the observed incident state were not reproduced |
| Waiting locally | The CI queue was stuck, and the local results were not used further | Held off on recording the local results as evidence of recovery | Local state cannot substitute for the actual consumer path |
| User path restored | Used Fang Ke to continue retrieving records from the original entry point | Recorded the recovery time separately from root-cause confirmation | It was not confirmed that all adopters had taken the same path |
| Interface check | There were ordering inversions between events, objects used in caller integration testing, and indexing times | Retained the unexplained time differences | It is not yet possible to determine whether the inversion occurred in the records or in entry-point selection |

The early records presented "user-path recovery" and "the issue has been resolved" as too closely linked. Looking back, the former only indicates that the path in question became usable again at that time; the latter requires, at a minimum, confirmation of whether the old relationships have disappeared, whether the entry point still lists two current records side by side, and whether the indexing times can be explained. The old records were not deleted, because they explain why the on-call staff stopped retrying.

## The entry point is not a single object

This anomaly was later broken down into three closely related but non-equivalent observations:

1. **Normal navigation path.** LPRB-005 started with a break in the navigation path for the current revision and required actual consumers to enter through that entry point and record the first broken link. The only concern here is where the path breaks.
2. **Withdrawal of old relationships.** LPRB-007 focuses on whether the old edges actually disappear after the exit action. It does not call for redoing all integration testing, but is intended to prevent the entry point from continuing to display the same material because of old relationships after the withdrawal.
3. **Indexing time.** LPRB-011 focuses on the ordering inversions between events, objects used in caller integration testing, and indexing times. Even if the entry point opens, the inversion still makes it difficult to explain what "current" points to.

Lumping three things together as "the entry point did not refresh" was a shortcoming of the first version. They can occur simultaneously around a single entry point, but the results of addressing them differ: navigation can be restored while the old relationship remains; the old relationship can be retracted while the indexing time still cannot be explained; the indexing order can be corrected, while consumers may still follow another broken-link path from a directory or report.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Caller entry point in a directory or report] --> B[Navigation for the current revision]
    B --> C{Can the revision be distinguished}
    C -- No --> D[Save the records shown at the entry point]
    D --> E[Check whether the old relationship has been retracted]
    D --> F[Check the indexing time]
    C -- Yes --> G{Actual consumer path restored}
    E --> H{Old edge has disappeared}
    F --> I{Time difference can be explained}
    G -- No --> J[Record the first broken-link location]
    G -- Yes --> K[Record only the recovery status]
    H -- No --> L[Keep the retraction issue]
    I -- No --> M[List the time difference separately]
```

The branches in the diagram are intended to preserve the order of judgments made at the time, not to indicate that a permanent troubleshooting procedure has been established. In particular, "being able to distinguish the revision" and "restoring the actual consumer path" are not interchangeable: the former concerns the two records displayed at the entry point, while the latter concerns whether consumers can still reach the original record.

## Section on retracting the old relationship

The follow-up action from LPRB-007 was to replay the retraction using the exit action corresponding to "the two record versions were not merged", and check whether the old edge had actually disappeared. The sample has been attached to that card; a later public note stated that this round's expiration action came from the hot cache.

This explanation belongs only in the section on the old relationship. It can explain why the display after retraction still carries the old state, and also reminds us not to conclude from a single displayed result that the old edge is still present; but it cannot replace checking the actual relationships at the entry point, much less explain factory scope. The earlier description of "hot cache" as the cause of the entire anomaly was an overly broad attribution, and it has now been revised to keep it in its original local context.

The retraction check itself also cannot be replaced by "user path recovery". When consumers regain access, the entry point may simply have happened to select a readable record; whether the old edge has disappeared remains a separate fact. Conversely, even if the old edge is no longer displayed, the directory or report may still contain paths that break before reaching the original entry point.

## Section on indexing time

The observation in LPRB-011 was that the order between the indexing time and the caller's integration-testing target was reversed. The interface check had already taken place, but the reversal was not directly attributed to an implementation error. The existing records can only establish this: the sequences shown in the two record views cannot naturally be pieced together into a single linear timeline.

The same shift log specified different expiry actions on the two sides, invalidating the shortcut of "treat the newer entry as authoritative". An earlier version tried to explain the different actions as a data-entry delay; this explanation is no longer retained as a conclusion, because no evidence shows which action was adopted first, and no evidence shows that the other entry was merely an outdated copy.

Therefore, when a timing difference cannot explain the discrepancy, it remains listed separately, rather than being smoothed over by changing the entry-point text. The entry-point instructions should only tell readers whether they can reach the current record; they should not add an unsupported sequence of events to the index records.

## User Paths and Evidence Quality

LPRB-009 require navigating from the directory or report to the original record for the current revision, and writing back the location of the first broken link. This requirement adds a perspective missing from the first version: just because the current entry point on the page looks usable does not mean actual users enter from the same starting point.

A secondhand account consisting only of screenshots had previously been used to show that another path was working normally. It did not retain the context needed to identify the corresponding entry-point version, and was later no longer used to explain path differences. It can still show that someone saw a working result at the time, but it cannot support the broader conclusion that "the other path was working normally".

The handling of LPRB-013 is also related to this: the navigation entry point for the current revision can remain, while explanatory text that cannot be traced back should be removed. Here, "removed" does not mean erasing history, but preventing the entry page from passing off speculation as explanation. The two original versions of the record and this postmortem remain available for anyone who needs to look back and understand the sequence of events on site.

## Backfilled Entries and Board Sequence

Subsequent actions took this beyond a simple entry-point failure, to the point where the sequence of records also needed to be preserved. LPRB-005 had already completed scope confirmation, then became blocked because the CI queue stalled. The local results remained on site but were not used for further assessment; this was not because the local results were being rejected, but because they had not gone through the step in which actual users obtain the materials through the entry point.

The sample for LPRB-007 was attached before the withdrawal replay. This sample shows that the old relationship warrants a separate check, but did not provide the complete state of the entry point after the old edge disappeared. When work later resumed, the withdrawal action remained a local verification item, and "replayed" must not be written as "the two records have already been proven to be separate".

The interface check for LPRB-011 subsequently entered review. The explanation for the backfilled board entry is: the submission for the caller's core-module integration testing preceded the board sync, and the item went straight into review after it was backfilled. This sequence explains why the board item is not suitable for establishing the timeline on its own, but it does not explain why the order of the index timestamps is reversed relative to the caller's integration-testing targets. Both types of timing information continue to be retained side by side, to avoid substituting board status for the relationships between records seen at the entry point.

The sample for LPRB-013 was attached later, and it concerns a source-less explanation of the current revision. It did not ask for navigation to be removed, nor did it change the historical fact that the two revisions once shared an entry point. After the explanatory text is cleaned up, the entry point may still need the old relationships and timing reviewed; therefore, "the explanation has been moved" does not mean the issue is closed.

## Breakdown of recovery states

When the old version used "recovery," it did not specify which layer had recovered, making it easy for readers to extrapolate one green status to other parts. The states observed in the field are now separated as follows:

| Name | What it could explain at the time | What it could not explain |
|---|---|---|
| wrapper lifecycle recovery | The observed lifecycle-related state was later restored | Does not indicate the index, old relationships, or which revision it belongs to |
| User path recovery | A particular consumer path could retrieve the record again | Does not indicate that all consumers entered through the same entry point |
| Current entry point can be opened | The entry point did not break during that inspection | Does not indicate that only one revision remained in the entry point |
| Old relationship withdrawal complete | Must be confirmed separately using the state of the old edge after replay | A single successful display should not be treated as a substitute |

This breakdown preserves the observation from the first version but withdraws the inference that "delayed lifecycle recovery was the cause." At the time, that sentence merely linked two similar phenomena; the fact that the entry point could still later contain mixed records shows that this link was insufficient to explain the entire anomaly.

## Use of DOC-33

DOC-33 is adjacent migration material for the current entry point. It can help review the entry-point context left by the migration, but it does not establish the cause of this incident. This page is concerned only with the observed fact that the two revisions did not merge at the current entry point; judgments in the migration material cannot be directly repurposed as explanations for old relationships, index timing, or factory scope.

This distinction also affects the review order. When confirming the normal navigation chain, first retrace it from the directory or report and record the first broken-link location; when confirming old relationships, inspect the old edge after replaying the withdrawal; when discussing index inversion, inspect the time discrepancy recorded by the interface check. DOC-33 can provide historical context for the adjacent entry point, but it will not combine the three checks into a single result.

## Remaining open scope

The following questions are not a generalized version of the task list; they are gaps left directly by this incident:

| Question | Available material | What is still missing |
|---|---|---|
| Why factory scope changed | Old records do not match the material seen at the entry point | The change cannot be traced to a revision, an index, or a withdrawal action |
| Whether the old relationships have disappeared completely | Withdrawal replay and additional samples are available | Still need to confirm that the entry point will not show another revision alongside it again |
| Where the index timing inversion occurred | Interface checks are complete, and the time difference has been identified | There is not enough material to determine whether it is due to record order or entry point selection |
| How broad adoption is | Actual consumers have been asked to retrace the path from the directory or report | It has not been confirmed that all adopters start from the same point |

While the CI queue was blocked, local results were not used for further assessment, and this point should still be retained. It was neither a cause of the incident nor a recovery action; it explains why local results were not used at the time to broaden the conclusions further. If new execution results become available later, they should be distinguished from this waiting period and must not be retroactively written in as evidence that had already been seen at the time.

## How the old conclusions are retained

"The old index was not refreshed", "Lifecycle recovery was delayed", and "Data entry was delayed" were all working assessments made during the incident. The first statement remains a possible line of suspicion regarding the entry point relationship; the latter two can no longer serve as a complete explanation. These statements are retained not so that they can continue to be used, but because removing them would make the subsequent checks of old relationships, checks of index timing, and cleanup of unsourced explanations appear to have come out of nowhere.

Likewise, the configuration identity mismatch remains the earliest visible deviation, but it is not the only field used to determine the associated revision. classloader ownership showed no anomalies at the time, which indicates that the initial comparison did not point to a problem there, but does not prove that there were no problems in other layers. This limitation was not made clear in earlier versions and is now being added here.

DOC-33 document adjacent entry point migration material; this postmortem references it only when revisiting the migration context and does not recast the migration assessments in that material as the cause of this anomaly. The two documents are kept separate precisely because this page focuses on the fact that the two revisions were not merged at the current entry point, rather than on the results of all entry point migrations.

## Currently available conclusions

As of this version, the only conclusions that can reliably be retained are these: the two revisions were present at the current entry point at the same time; configuration identity differed from the old records; both the user path and wrapper lifecycle had recovered; the old relationships, index timing, and adoption scope each still have unconfirmed items. Explanations beyond these should still not be presented as root causes.

If consumers encounter the same entry point again, first determine whether the chain breaks before reaching the entry point from the directory or report, or whether revisions cannot be distinguished within the entry point. For the former, retain the location of the first break in the chain; for the latter, retain the records seen at the entry point, the state of the old relationships, and the index timing together. Do not overwrite the two earlier versions of the material merely because one path has recovered.

This page is retained as a postmortem from the old entry point era. It does not cover entry point implementations that may have appeared later, nor does it present the still-unconfirmed change in factory scope as a resolved issue.

# Dependency Boundary Failure Runbook

## Before starting

This on-call shift handles only one run of `license-supply-boundary`. First open `docs/adj-license/runbooks/LICENSE-dependency-boundary-audit-one-failed-run-on-call-page.md` and confirm that the object, boundary, and page record at hand belong to the same run. If the file cannot be opened, or the object does not match the page contents, stop at the entry point, record the object and file path actually observed, and do not continue with the checks below.

## On-site sequence

1. In that file, find `compatibility matrix`, then first verify the adopted scope already recorded for this run. Leave windows with no record blank; do not infer from adjacent steps.
2. As soon as you see `statement replacement` during the run, first record the step and object where it appeared. Do not clean up the scene, and do not write this result directly as a final success or failure.
3. Return to the page record and check `rollback checkpoint`. If the checkpoint does not appear, stop here. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment; do not treat the old entry point as a verified fallback path yet.
4. If the record points to `classloader ownership`, retain this judgment term and the corresponding failing step. First have the person who maintains that entry point confirm it; do not rewrite the ownership on this page.

## How to record

Each drill changes only one condition. Each added entry must include at least: the adopted boundary, the actual object, the first failure to appear, whether `statement replacement` was seen, and whether `rollback checkpoint` exists. Keep time periods with no record in between blank; do not fill them with results from the preceding or following steps.

`wrapper lifecycle` is retained only as a locator for this session. It cannot replace a step or indicate that recovery is complete. If the page and the on-site state are inconsistent again, stop at the first inconsistency and preserve the failing step, specific object, and file path. When the next shift takes over, continue checking from there first; do not overwrite the original record.

## After stopping

After stopping, write back to this page where the failure occurred, the items not yet confirmed, and the windows that are still blank. The entry file and attachments remain maintained by `adj-license`; if the recovery action has not been tested, record "not tested" and do not add a speculative success result. Record subsequent changes related to this boundary in a new record, preserving the original stopping point here.
